blocks.html: This course walks from the cave painters to the late Renaissance. Before the walk starts, you need one habit that works for every work you will meet: formal analysis. "Form" here means how a work is made: its line, shape, color, light, space, composition, scale and material. Formal analysis looks hard at those things first and saves the question of meaning for last.

Art historians often work in three steps. Describe: say plainly what is there, so that anyone looking would agree. Analyze: say how the parts are arranged and what that does to your eye. Interpret: say what the work might mean, pointing back to what you described. (The Color and Design course adds a fourth step, judging.)
Describe what you see, analyze how it is arranged, then interpret what it might mean. Every claim about meaning should point to something you can see.

Description is the evidence. "This painting is about wealth" is a guess until you can say why: the fur, the imported oranges, the brass chandelier. Describing first also slows you down, so you notice details a quick glance misses.

blocks.cap: Jan van Eyck, The Arnolfini Portrait, 1434. Tap the numbers, and zoom in on the mirror.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Arnolfini Portrait. It is small, about 82 by 60 centimeters, painted in oil on an oak panel. A man and a woman stand in a room lit by a window at the left. They are in rich clothes: his fur-trimmed dark robe and tall hat, her green gown lined with fur. Their hands meet at the center. Lines of the floorboards and the bed run back toward the mirror, so the eye travels into the room and lands on the tiny reflection. The colors are deep and glowing, and the light catches brass, glass and fur in different ways. That is the description and analysis. Only now do we interpret: the picture shows wealth and a formal moment between two people. Scholars still debate whether it records a marriage, a betrothal or something else.

head: Look at
Ask yourself
rows: Where are the strong edges? Straight or curved?
Where does the light come from? Which colors repeat?
Is it flat or deep? What is near and what is far?
Where is the focal point? What leads your eye there?
How big is it? What is it made of, and how does that show?
blocks.cap: A checklist for describing and analyzing.

blocks.title: Three steps with one detail
blocks.q: Use the three steps on the mirror in the Arnolfini Portrait.
steps: Describe. A round, curved mirror hangs on the back wall in a frame with ten small scenes. In it we see the couple from behind and two figures in a doorway.
Analyze. It sits near the center, just above the joined hands, and the room's lines lead to it. Its curve bends the whole room into a small circle.
Interpret. The two figures stand where a visitor would stand. With the words "Jan van Eyck was here" above, many think one of them is the painter, a witness to the scene.
blocks.a: Describe the mirror and its reflection, analyze its place and its curve, then interpret the figures as possible witnesses.

blocks.html: Jumping to the story or the artist's life before looking. Facts about Van Eyck are useful, but they are not a description of this painting. Check yourself: could someone who has never read about the work agree with each of your first sentences?

blocks.html: Three words help you sort any picture: subject, genre and style. They answer different questions, so keep them apart.

items: Subject: what the work shows. A man and his hounds coming home in the snow. A woman pouring milk.

Genre: the family of subjects it belongs to. The main genres of European painting are history painting (stories from religion, myth, history or literature), portrait, genre scene (everyday life), landscape and still life.
Style: how it is shown. Flat or deep, smooth or brushy, calm or dramatic. A period style (Gothic, Renaissance) is shared by many artists; a personal style belongs to one.

blocks.html: Subject is what is shown; genre is the kind of subject; style is how it is shown.

Genre tells you what a picture was for and how people of its time ranked it. In the academies of the 1600s and later, history painting stood at the top, with portraits next, then genre scenes, landscapes and still lifes. Knowing the genre helps you ask the right questions: a portrait raises the question of likeness; a history painting raises the question of which story.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Pieter Bruegel the Elder, Hunters in the Snow, 1565.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Hunters in the Snow. Three hunters and their dogs trudge downhill at the left, past a fire outside an inn. The hill drops away to a wide valley of frozen ponds, where tiny figures skate, and on to jagged mountains. Dark tree trunks and dark figures stand out against white snow and a green-gray sky, and a long diagonal carries your eye from the hunters to the far distance. The subject is a winter day; the genre is landscape with everyday life in it; the style is Bruegel's: crisp outlines, a high viewpoint and a huge, carefully built space.

blocks.cap: Johannes Vermeer, The Milkmaid, about 1660. A genre scene from the next course.

blocks.html: Vermeer's Milkmaid is a genre scene: a kitchen maid pours milk at a table by a window. You will meet it again in Art History II.

blocks.title: Sort one painting
blocks.q: Leonardo's Mona Lisa: what are its subject, genre and style?
steps: Subject: a seated woman with folded hands, before a distant landscape.
Genre: it shows a particular person, so it is a portrait.
Style: soft, smoky shading without hard outlines (sfumato), typical of Leonardo and the High Renaissance.
blocks.a: Subject: a seated woman; genre: portrait; style: Leonardo's soft High Renaissance modeling.

blocks.html: Calling every type of painting a "genre painting." In art history, genre painting means one genre: scenes of everyday life, like the Milkmaid. A landscape is a genre, but it is not a genre painting. Check: does it show ordinary people doing ordinary things? Then it is a genre scene.

blocks.html: Paint is two things: pigment (colored powder, often ground minerals) and a binder that holds it and sticks it to a surface. Change the binder and you change everything: how fast the paint dries, how you can work with it, and how it looks centuries later.

blocks.html: Fresco is painted into wet plaster; tempera is pigment in egg; oil is pigment in slow-drying oil that can be blended and glazed.

In true fresco, lime in the plaster reacts with the air as it dries and locks the pigment into a thin crust of stone. That is why frescoes survive on walls for centuries, and why the painter has only hours before the patch sets. Oil dries slowly because the oil hardens by slowly taking up oxygen from the air, which leaves days to blend.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Fra Angelico, The Annunciation, about 1440 to 1445, fresco, Convent of San Marco, Florence.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Fra Angelico's Annunciation. An angel with striped wings bows to a seated young woman in a simple porch of slender columns and arches. The colors are pale and clear, the forms simple, the background garden flat and quiet. That matte, chalky clarity is typical of true fresco. It was painted at the top of a staircase in a friars' convent, so the friars saw it every time they climbed to their rooms.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Leonardo da Vinci, The Last Supper, about 1495 to 1498, Milan.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Last Supper's surface. Leonardo wanted to work slowly and blend like a panel painter, so he did not paint true fresco. He used tempera and oil on a dry wall. The paint began flaking within decades. What you see today is the result of many repairs and a long restoration finished in 1999.

blocks.title: Which medium?
blocks.q: A painter wants to soften the edge of a cheek over several days and lay thin, glowing layers of color. Which medium fits best?
steps: Fresco sets within a day, so no.
Tempera dries in minutes and is built in small strokes, so blending is hard.
Oil stays workable for days and can be glazed.
blocks.a: Oil paint.

blocks.html: Calling every wall painting a fresco. True fresco is painted into wet plaster. The Last Supper is a wall painting but not a true fresco, and that is part of why it decayed so fast. Check: was the paint applied wet into fresh plaster? If not, it is secco or another wall technique.

blocks.html: Sculptors work in three basic ways. They carve (take material away from stone, wood or ivory), model (build up a soft material such as clay or wax), or cast (pour liquid metal into a mold). Carving is called subtractive: once a piece is cut off, it is gone. Modeling is additive: you can keep adding.

Sculpture also comes in two kinds of space. Sculpture in the round stands free, and you can walk around it. Relief stays attached to a background, like a carving on a wall. Low relief barely rises from the surface; high relief stands far out.
Carve to take away, model to build up, cast to pour. Relief stays attached to a background; sculpture in the round stands free.

Most large bronzes are cast by the lost-wax process. The sculptor makes the figure in wax over a clay core, adds wax channels for the metal to flow in and for air to escape, and covers it all in a clay mold. Heating melts the wax out (the wax is "lost"), leaving a thin, hollow space. Molten bronze is poured in, the mold is broken away, and the metal is cleaned and polished. A hollow bronze is lighter and uses less metal, and large figures were often cast in several pieces and joined.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Charioteer of Delphi, about 475 BC, bronze. Delphi Archaeological Museum.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Charioteer of Delphi. A young man stands very straight in a long robe that falls in deep, regular folds like the flutes of a column. He once held the reins of a four-horse chariot that is now mostly lost. His eyes are inlaid glass and stone, and his lips and eyelashes were copper, so he once looked startlingly alive. The statue was cast in separate pieces by the lost-wax process and joined. A ruler of Gela in Sicily dedicated it to Apollo for a chariot victory.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Law Code Stele of Hammurabi, about 1750 BC, basalt. The top is carved in relief.

blocks.html: The Stele of Hammurabi shows relief: two figures carved at the top of a tall stone, still part of it, with the laws cut into the stone below.

blocks.title: Name the process
blocks.q: A Chinese ritual vessel of the Shang dynasty is bronze, and a Greek maiden statue is marble. How was each made?
steps: Bronze is a metal. Metal sculpture is shaped by melting and pouring: casting.
Marble is stone. Stone is shaped by cutting away: carving.
Shang bronze casters used molds made in sections, a different casting method from lost wax, but it is still casting.
blocks.a: The bronze vessel was cast; the marble statue was carved.

blocks.html: Thinking bronze statues are carved. Bronze is cast, usually by the lost-wax process, and then finished with tools. Check the material: stone and wood are carved; clay and wax are modeled; metal is cast.

blocks.html: Picture an artist alone in a studio, painting whatever comes to mind. For most of history it did not work that way. Art was commissioned: a patron asked for it, paid for it and often set its subject, size, materials and even how much gold or costly blue paint went into it. Patrons were kings and emperors, popes and bishops, monasteries, city councils, guilds and rich families such as the Medici of Florence.
Most art before modern times was made to order. Ask who paid for it, what it was for, and where it was meant to be seen.

A work makes more sense in its setting. A fresco at the top of a convent stair was made for friars to see daily. An altarpiece was made to stand over an altar during services. A small portrait might be a gift, a record or a memory. Knowing the patron and the place explains choices that look odd out of context: the size, the materials, who is shown, even who is left out.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Piero della Francesca, Portraits of the Duke and Duchess of Urbino, about 1473 to 1475. Uffizi Galleries, Florence.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Duke and Duchess of Urbino. Two profiles face each other across a wide landscape of hills and water, like two heads on a coin. Federico da Montefeltro, a soldier and patron of learning, wears red; Battista Sforza is pale, with jewels and pearls. Both are set high against a far, misty view, so they seem to rule over the land itself. Federico is always shown from this side: he had lost his right eye in a tournament. The backs of the panels show the couple riding in triumphal carts. These portraits were made for a court, to honor a ruling family. Battista died in 1472, so if the usual date is right, her portrait was a memorial; some scholars date the pair a few years earlier, while she was alive.

blocks.title: Read the context
blocks.q: In 1311 the people of Siena carried Duccio's huge altarpiece, the Maestà, in a procession through the city to their cathedral. What does that tell us about the work?
steps: It was made for the cathedral, to stand over the high altar.
The procession shows it mattered to the whole city, not only to clergy.
Its size, its gold and its scenes were chosen for that public, sacred place.
blocks.a: It was a civic and religious commission, made for Siena's cathedral and honored by the whole city.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Duccio di Buoninsegna, Maestà, 1308 to 1311, tempera and gold on wood. Siena.

blocks.html: Museum labels look certain, but every date and every name on them is a conclusion from evidence. Art historians use four main kinds of evidence. Documents: contracts, payments, letters and inventories. The object itself: signatures, dates and inscriptions. Style: how the work compares with ones whose dates are known. Science: radiocarbon dating of charcoal or wood (for things up to about 50,000 years old), tree rings in wooden panels, X-rays and infrared images that show drawing under the paint, and tests of the pigments.

head: On a label
What it means
rows: The year is known, usually from a dated signature or a document.
Made over several years, or dated somewhere in that span.
Scholars think this artist made it, but it is not proven.
Made in the master's workshop, by assistants, perhaps with the master.
A name or identity is a guess.
blocks.cap: Reading a label.

blocks.html: A date or a name on a label is a conclusion, and the wording tells you how sure scholars are. "c." means about; "attributed to" means likely but not certain.

Before about 1400 most European artists did not sign their work, and outside Europe many traditions never did. So we often know a workshop, a city or a culture rather than a person. Style can place a work within a few decades; documents can pin it to a day. When the evidence conflicts, the label says so.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Jan van Eyck, Portrait of a Man (Self Portrait?), 1433. National Gallery, London.

blocks.html: Looking closely: A man in a red turban. A man of middle age looks out from a dark ground, his face lit from the left with every crease and stubble hair painted. The red cloth piled on his head is folded and twisted into a sculptural shape. The original frame is painted with words: "Jan van Eyck made me in the year 1433 on 21 October," and at the top his motto, "As I can." The date is certain. Whether the man is Van Eyck himself is not: many scholars think so, partly because of the motto and the direct gaze, so the title ends with a question mark.

blocks.title: Read the label
blocks.q: The National Gallery calls a Titian portrait "Portrait of Gerolamo (?) Barbarigo." What do you know, and what don't you know?
steps: The painter: the museum gives it to Titian with no "attributed to," so it is accepted as his.
The sitter: the question mark means the name Gerolamo Barbarigo is a guess.
In fact, the man was once called the poet Ariosto, and some think it is Titian himself.
blocks.a: Titian is accepted as the painter; who the sitter was is uncertain.

blocks.cap: Titian, Portrait of a Man, about 1510. National Gallery, London.

blocks.html: Reading "c. 1500" as an exact year, or "attributed to" as proven. Both labels are telling you how sure scholars are. Check the wording before you quote a date or a name, and keep the "about."

blocks.html: The oldest paintings we know are deep inside caves. In southern France, the walls of Chauvet Cave carry horses, lions, rhinoceroses and mammoths painted about 36,000 years ago, according to radiocarbon tests of the charcoal. The paintings of Lascaux, also in France, are younger, about 17,000 years old. In northern Spain, the cave of Altamira is famous for its painted bison.

The painters used what the earth gave them: red, yellow and brown ochre (iron oxides), black from charcoal or manganese oxide, mixed with water or fat. They painted with fingers, pads of moss or fur, and brushes of hair, and they blew paint through hollow bones or reeds to make hand stencils. They worked by the light of torches and stone lamps that burned animal fat.
Paleolithic painters made closely observed animals deep in caves, with mineral pigments and charcoal: Chauvet about 36,000 years ago, Lascaux about 17,000.

How do we know the age of a painting? Charcoal is burned wood, and wood was once alive, so radiocarbon dating can tell how long ago that tree died, up to about 50,000 years. Red and yellow ochre has no carbon, so those paintings are dated by nearby finds, by charcoal in the same layers, or by mineral crusts that formed on top of them.

blocks.cap: The Hall of the Bulls, Lascaux, about 17,000 years ago.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Hall of the Bulls. Huge aurochs, horses and deer cross the pale, uneven rock in every direction. Nothing is lined up on a floor; animals overlap and float, some upside down to each other. The black outlines are bold and sure, drawn in long sweeps, while other animals are filled with red or brown. The painters knew these animals well: the hump of a back, the sweep of a horn, the slim legs of a deer. The cave was found in 1940 by four teenagers. Visitors' breath and lights damaged it, so it was closed in 1963; people now visit full-size copies nearby.

blocks.title: Why the inside of a cave?
blocks.q: Lascaux's paintings are far from daylight. What does that suggest about their purpose?
steps: People did not live deep in caves; they lived near entrances or in the open.
So the paintings were not everyday decoration of a home.
Scholars have proposed ritual, hunting magic, storytelling and the work of shamans. No one knows for sure.
blocks.a: They were probably made for special purposes, perhaps ritual; the exact purpose is still debated.

blocks.html: Imagining cave art as crude scribbles. Look again: the animals are observed closely, drawn with confident lines, and often placed so that a bulge in the rock becomes a shoulder or a belly. These painters were skilled artists.
Cave art is not only European. A hand stencil in a cave on the island of Sulawesi, Indonesia, is at least 40,000 years old.

blocks.html: Paintings on cave walls stay where they are. But Ice Age people also made art they could hold and carry: small carvings in ivory, bone, antler and stone, and the first musical instruments, flutes made from bird bone and ivory. Archaeologists call this portable art. Some of it is older than any known cave painting.

The most famous piece is the Lion-Man of Hohlenstein-Stadel, from a cave in the Swabian Jura of southern Germany. It is a figure about 31 centimeters tall, carved from a mammoth tusk about 40,000 years ago. It stands upright like a person, but its head is a cave lion's. It is now in the Museum Ulm. (We do not have an approved picture of it yet, so here it is described in words.)
Carved figures are among the oldest art in the world. The Lion-Man, carved from mammoth ivory about 40,000 years ago, is part human and part lion.

A creature that is part animal and part human does not exist in nature. To carve one, someone had to imagine it first. That is why archaeologists see the Lion-Man as evidence of imagination and perhaps of shared stories or beliefs, tens of thousands of years ago.

Looking closely: The Lion-Man. It is long and narrow, shaped by the curve of the tusk. The head has the short muzzle and small ears of a big cat; the body stands upright on two legs, with arms held at its sides, and a few lines are cut into its surface. Carving it with stone tools would have taken many hours of careful work, since ivory is hard and splits easily. It was found in 1939 as some 200 broken fragments, put together in the 1960s and 1980s, and rebuilt again after more pieces were found in 2008 and later.

head: Clue
What it tells us
rows: Carvers used the big animals of the Ice Age for material as well as food.
The community valued it enough to spare the time.
Imagination: a creature no one had seen.
Perhaps a special place; its use is unknown.
blocks.cap: Reading the Lion-Man as evidence.

blocks.title: Which came first?
blocks.q: Is the Lion-Man older or younger than the paintings of Lascaux?
steps: Lion-Man: about 40,000 years ago.
Lascaux: about 17,000 years ago.
40,000 is more than twice 17,000, so the Lion-Man is much older.
blocks.a: Older, by more than 20,000 years.

blocks.html: Assuming the oldest art must be painting. Carved figures are at least as old as the oldest cave paintings we know. Check the dates, not your expectations.

After farming spread across Europe, Neolithic people began to raise enormous stones. Megalith means "great stone" in Greek. They built circles, rows and tombs. At Newgrange in Ireland, about 3200 BC, a passage tomb lines up so that sunlight at dawn on the winter solstice shines down its long passage into the chamber.

The most famous megalithic monument is Stonehenge on Salisbury Plain in England. It was built in stages, from a circular ditch and bank about 3000 BC to the great stones about 2500 BC, with changes until about 1500 BC.
Stonehenge was built in stages from about 3000 to 1500 BC by Neolithic and Bronze Age people. Its axis lines up with the midsummer sunrise and the midwinter sunset.

Stonehenge has two kinds of stone. The huge sarsens, many of them about 25 tons, came from West Woods, about 25 kilometers away. The smaller bluestones came from the Preseli Hills in Wales, more than 200 kilometers away. Moving them with ropes, sledges and many hands took planning and a lot of people working together, which is itself evidence of an organized society.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Stonehenge, Wiltshire, England, about 3000 to 1500 BC.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Stonehenge. Upright stones stand in a ring, some still capped by flat stones laid across their tops. Inside stand five giant pairs, each with its own top stone: trilithons, "three stones." The builders treated stone like timber. They shaped knobs (tenons) on the uprights to fit hollows (mortises) under the lintels, and fitted the lintels end to end with tongue-and-groove joints, the way a carpenter joins wood. The lintels are even shaped to follow the curve of the circle.

blocks.title: Who built it?
blocks.q: A guidebook says the Druids built Stonehenge. Check the dates.
steps: The great stones went up about 2500 BC.
Druids were priests of the Iron Age Celts, first described in Greek and Roman writings many centuries later.
So Stonehenge stood for well over a thousand years before there were Druids.
blocks.a: The Druids did not build it; it is far older than they are.

blocks.html: Crediting the Druids with Stonehenge. The idea came from writers of the 1600s and 1700s. Radiocarbon dates show it was built more than a thousand years before the Druids are recorded. Check: compare the monument's dates with the dates of the people named.

Why was it built? The main ideas are a ceremonial site, a burial place (cremated remains were buried there) and a marker of the solstices. These are not exclusive, and scholars still debate the balance.

blocks.html: Mesopotamia, "the land between the rivers," is the plain of the Tigris and Euphrates in what is now Iraq. Here, by about 3500 BC, people built some of the first cities and invented writing: cuneiform, wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay. Stone was scarce, so they built with mud brick, and they put their temples high.

A ziggurat is a huge stepped platform of mud brick with a temple on top, the house of a city's god. The Ziggurat of Ur was built about 2100 BC by King Ur-Nammu for Nanna, the moon god. Its core is sun-dried mud brick, wrapped in a thick skin of baked brick set in bitumen (natural tar) to keep the rain out. Long stairways led up to the shrine.
Mesopotamian builders raised mud-brick ziggurats as platforms for temples, and carved steles: tall stone slabs with pictures and writing, like the Stele of Hammurabi.

Why build so high? A high temple was closer to the sky where the gods lived, and it could be seen from far across the flat plain. Mud brick crumbles in rain, so a solid, stepped mass with a hard outer skin was the strongest way to stack it high.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Stele of Hammurabi. A tall, black, finger-shaped stone. At the top, in relief, King Hammurabi of Babylon stands with his hand raised to his mouth in respect before Shamash, who sits on a throne with rays rising from his shoulders. Shamash is larger: even seated, he is nearly as tall as the standing king. Below, the rest of the stone is covered with neat columns of cuneiform, 282 laws, each in the form "if someone does this, then that follows." The picture makes the message plain to anyone, reader or not: the laws come with the authority of the god. The stele was carried off to Susa, in Iran, as war booty in the 1100s BC, where French archaeologists found it in 1901.

blocks.title: Ziggurat or pyramid?
blocks.q: Both are huge stepped or sloped mountains of material. How do a ziggurat and an Egyptian pyramid differ in purpose?
steps: A ziggurat is a platform with a temple on top; people climbed it by stairs.
An Egyptian pyramid is a tomb for a king, sealed, with the burial inside.
Also: ziggurats are mud brick; the pyramids of Giza are stone.
blocks.a: A ziggurat holds up a temple; a pyramid holds a royal burial.

blocks.html: Mixing up a ziggurat with an Egyptian pyramid. A ziggurat is a stepped platform with a temple on top, not a tomb. Check: is there a shrine on top and a stair to reach it? Then it is a ziggurat.

blocks.html: Three great empires followed in the Near East. The Assyrians ruled from palaces in northern Mesopotamia in the 800s and 700s BC. The Neo-Babylonians rebuilt Babylon in the 500s BC. Then the Persians built an empire from Egypt to India and a ceremonial capital at Persepolis. Each used art to show the ruler's power to everyone who came to the palace.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: A pair of lamassu from the palace of Ashurnasirpal II at Nimrud, 883 to 859 BC. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The lamassu. A lamassu is a protective spirit with a bearded man's head, a horned crown, eagle wings and the body of a lion or bull. Pairs of them, carved in huge stone blocks, flanked palace doorways. Look at the legs. From the front, the creature stands still on two legs. From the side, it strides forward on four. To make both views complete, the sculptors gave it five legs. The carving is crisp and patterned: curls of beard and hair, rows of feathers.
Assyrian palaces were guarded by lamassu; Babylon's Ishtar Gate glowed with blue glazed brick; Persepolis shows rows of gift bearers from every part of the Persian Empire.

The five legs answer a question about viewpoints. A guardian at a door is seen first from the front as you approach and then from the side as you pass. The sculptors chose to make each view correct rather than to make one physical animal, the same choice of clarity over a single viewpoint you will see in Egyptian art.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Ishtar Gate of Babylon, about 575 BC, rebuilt from the excavated bricks in the Pergamon Museum, Berlin.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Ishtar Gate. King Nebuchadnezzar II built this gate in the inner wall of Babylon. Its bricks were molded in relief and glazed deep blue, with rows of yellow-and-brown animals striding across: bulls for the storm god Adad and dragons for Babylon's god Marduk, while lions lined the walls of the Processional Way that led to it. Glaze is glass fused onto fired clay, so the colors did not fade. German archaeologists excavated the bricks between 1899 and 1917, and the gate was rebuilt in Berlin, partly from originals and partly with new bricks.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Apadana stairway reliefs, Persepolis, Iran, about 515 to 465 BC. A photograph of the 1800s.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The stairway at Persepolis. Darius I began Persepolis around 518 BC. Along the stairs of his great audience hall, the Apadana, file after file of men in different dress climb in low relief, carrying gifts: vessels, cloth, animals. They are delegations from the peoples of the empire, separated by carved trees. No one fights; everyone brings something. The message is order and harmony under the king. Persepolis was burned after Alexander the Great captured it in 330 BC.

blocks.title: Count the legs
blocks.q: Seen from the side, a lamassu has four legs walking. Seen from the front, it has two standing. How many legs are carved in all?
steps: From the front you see the two front legs.
From the side you see four legs, and one of them is a front leg you already counted.
So the side adds three more: 2 + 3 = 5.
blocks.a: Five legs.

blocks.html: Thinking a lamassu has four legs. Many have five, so they look complete from the front and from the side. Check by counting from each viewpoint.

sources.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York: Human-headed winged lion (lamassu), 883 to 859 BC

blocks.html: Egyptian art kept the same basic rules for nearly three thousand years. Learn the rules and you can read any Egyptian painting or relief.

items: Composite view. Each part of the body is shown from its clearest angle: the head in profile, but the eye drawn as if from the front; the shoulders from the front; the hips, legs and feet in profile.
Hierarchical scale. Size shows importance. A king or a god is drawn larger than the people around him.
Registers. Scenes are stacked in horizontal bands, each with its own ground line, read like lines of text.
The grid. Artists laid out figures on a grid of squares so that proportions came out the same. A standing figure was 18 squares from the soles of the feet to the hairline.

blocks.html: Egyptian artists showed each part of a figure in its clearest view, used size to show importance, arranged scenes in registers, and laid out figures on a grid.

These pictures were made for tombs and temples, to last forever and to work: a person shown complete and clearly could live on in the afterlife. A foot hidden behind another, or a face turned away, would leave something out. Clarity mattered more than how things look from one spot.

blocks.name: ar-artwork

hotspots.label: Composite view
hotspots.text: Hunefer: head in profile, eye seen from the front, shoulders turned toward us, legs in profile.

hotspots.label: The scales
hotspots.text: Anubis weighs Hunefer's heart against a feather standing for truth (Maat).

hotspots.label: Ammit
hotspots.text: A creature that would devour an unworthy heart.

hotspots.label: Thoth
hotspots.text: The ibis-headed god of writing records the result.

hotspots.label: Osiris
hotspots.text: Enthroned in a shrine, he receives Hunefer.

hotspots.label: The upper register
hotspots.text: Hunefer kneels before a row of seated gods.

blocks.cap: From the Book of the Dead of Hunefer, about 1275 BC, paint on papyrus. British Museum, London.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Weighing of the Heart. The scene reads left to right like a strip. Hunefer, in a white pleated robe, is led in by the jackal-headed god Anubis. In the middle, his heart is weighed on a great scale against a feather; the ibis-headed god Thoth writes down the result, and a beast waits below the scale. The heart balances, so the falcon-headed god Horus leads Hunefer to Osiris on his throne. Every figure stands on a firm ground line, every outline is clear, and the flat colors are keyed: white robes, green and blue for the gods. Hieroglyphs fill the spaces and label the scene. Above, a second register shows Hunefer kneeling before the gods.

blocks.title: Read the figure
blocks.q: In an Egyptian relief, a man's face is in profile but his eye is drawn as an almond shape seen from the front. Is this a mistake?
steps: A profile eye is a small sideways wedge, hard to read.
A frontal eye is the clearest view of an eye.
The artist chose the clearest view of each part: this is composite view, on purpose.
blocks.a: No: it is composite view, the clearest view of each part.

blocks.html: Thinking Egyptians could not draw realistically. They could; animals, birds and some servants in Egyptian art are strikingly lifelike. The rules showed important figures in their clearest, most complete form on purpose, and the rules lasted three thousand years. The Egyptology Ladder has a full lesson on the grid.
One short period broke the rules: under King Akhenaten (about 1353 to 1336 BC), Amarna art showed longer, softer, more relaxed figures. You will meet it in Temples and the New Kingdom.

sources.name: British Museum, London: Papyrus of Hunefer, the Book of the Dead

blocks.html: Egypt's Old Kingdom (about 2700 to 2200 BC) was the age of the pyramids. The first was built for King Djoser at Saqqara, about 2630 BC: a step pyramid of six stacked platforms, designed by his official Imhotep. It grew out of the mastaba, a low, flat-topped tomb, stacked smaller and smaller. Within a century, builders had learned to make true pyramids with smooth sloping sides.

At Giza stand three great pyramids, for Khufu, his son Khafre, and Menkaure, built about 2600 to 2500 BC. The Great Pyramid of Khufu was about 146 meters tall when finished, built of some two million limestone blocks, and it was the tallest building on Earth for thousands of years. Each pyramid had a temple at its foot, joined by a causeway to a valley temple near the Nile.
The pyramids of Giza (about 2600 to 2500 BC) were royal tombs. The Great Sphinx, probably made for Khafre, lies beside the causeway to his pyramid.

A pyramid was more than a big grave. Its shape may echo the sun's rays slanting down to earth, and the mound from which, in Egyptian belief, the world first rose. The king was buried inside, with temples for offerings so that his spirit would be cared for forever.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The pyramids of Giza, about 2600 to 2500 BC.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The pyramids of Giza. Three huge, simple shapes rise from the desert, with smaller pyramids for queens beside them. The sides once had a smooth casing of fine white limestone, polished to shine in the sun; most of it was stripped away for building stone in later centuries, leaving the stepped core you see. The pyramids are aligned closely to north, south, east and west. Their power comes from geometry, size and plainness: no ornament at all on the outside.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Great Sphinx of Giza, about 2500 BC, with a pyramid behind.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Great Sphinx. A lion's body lies stretched out with a king's head wearing the striped royal headcloth. It is carved out of the bedrock itself: the builders left a knob of rock while quarrying around it and shaped it into a guardian. Most Egyptologists date it to Khafre's reign; a few argue for his father, Khufu.

blocks.title: Who built the pyramids?
blocks.q: A movie shows enslaved crowds whipped as they drag stones. What does the evidence say?
steps: Archaeologists found a workers' town at Giza, with bakeries, storerooms and housing.
Workers were buried in tombs near the pyramids, with goods for the afterlife: an honor, not something given to slaves.
Most Egyptologists now think crews of skilled builders and rotating teams of laborers did the work, fed and housed by the state.
blocks.a: Organized, paid-in-food crews, not slaves, according to most Egyptologists.

blocks.html: Thinking slaves built the pyramids. The idea goes back to the Greek writer Herodotus, 2,000 years after the fact. Evidence from the workers' town and tombs points to organized crews who were housed and fed. Check what kind of evidence supports a claim: a story told much later, or finds from the site itself?
The Egyptology Ladder's grid lesson and its history course go deeper into the Old Kingdom.

blocks.html: In the New Kingdom (about 1550 to 1070 BC), Egypt was an empire, and its kings poured their wealth into temples. They were buried in hidden rock-cut tombs in the Valley of the Kings, across the Nile from Thebes (modern Luxor), and built separate temples for their worship.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The temple of Hatshepsut at Deir el-Bahari, about 1479 to 1458 BC. An early photograph.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Hatshepsut's temple. Hatshepsut was a woman who ruled as king. Her temple rises in three broad terraces, linked by ramps, against a wall of cliffs. Long rows of square pillars make shadowed colonnades, and the horizontal lines answer the layers of the rock behind. Her steward Senenmut is traditionally credited with the design. The building fits its setting so well that it seems to grow out of the mountain.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Great Hypostyle Hall, Karnak, about 1290 to 1224 BC.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The hall at Karnak. A hypostyle hall is one whose roof rests on many columns. At Karnak, begun by Seti I and finished by Ramesses II, 134 columns stand in rows, the tallest down the center, carved like bundles of papyrus. Walking in once felt like walking through a stone marsh in near-darkness, lit only from high windows. Every surface was carved and painted.
New Kingdom kings built great temples such as Karnak and Hatshepsut's; the Amarna period produced the bust of Nefertiti, and Tutankhamun's tomb gave us his gold mask.

Why did the Amarna period look different? King Akhenaten worshiped one god, the sun disk Aten, and moved the capital to a new city, Amarna. Art changed with him: longer faces, softer bodies, scenes of the royal family at ease. After his death the old gods and the old style returned.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The bust of Nefertiti, about 1345 BC, painted limestone and stucco. Neues Museum, Berlin.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Nefertiti. Queen Nefertiti, Akhenaten's wife, wears a tall blue crown. Her long neck, fine features and smooth, even color make her look calm and perfect. One eye is inlaid with rock crystal; the other has no inlay, perhaps never added, which fits the idea that this was a model kept in the workshop of the sculptor Thutmose, where German archaeologists found it in 1912. It has been in Berlin since soon after, and today it is in the Neues Museum.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The mask of Tutankhamun, about 1323 BC, gold with inlays, in its coffin in 1925. Grand Egyptian Museum, Giza.

blocks.title: Why so famous?
blocks.q: Tutankhamun ruled only about ten years and died young. Why is he the best-known pharaoh today?
steps: Almost every royal tomb in the Valley of the Kings was robbed in ancient times.
His small tomb was found in 1922 by Howard Carter's team, nearly intact, with over 5,000 objects.
His solid gold mask, more than 10 kilograms, shows what a royal burial held.
blocks.a: Because his tomb survived nearly intact, not because of his reign.

blocks.html: Thinking Tutankhamun was a great pharaoh because his tomb is famous. He was a young king. His tomb is famous because it was found nearly intact. Check: is a work famous for its maker, or for how it survived?

blocks.html: Before Classical Greece came two Bronze Age civilizations around the Aegean Sea. The Minoans of Crete (named by a modern archaeologist after the legendary King Minos) built large palaces from about 1900 BC and traded across the sea. The Mycenaeans of mainland Greece built fortified citadels and were rich in gold; they took over Crete about 1450 BC.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The north entrance of the palace at Knossos, Crete, with a painted relief of a charging bull. Partly reconstructed in the early 1900s.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Knossos. The palace at Knossos was a huge cluster of rooms, stairways and light wells around a central court, so tangled that later Greeks may have remembered it as the Labyrinth of legend. Here you see red columns that are wider at the top than at the bottom, a Minoan habit, and a wall painting of a bull. Be careful: the archaeologist Arthur Evans, who dug the site from 1900, rebuilt parts of it in reinforced concrete and repainted them. Some of what visitors see is his reconstruction, and scholars still argue over how much is right.
Minoan art loved the sea and nature. Pots of the Marine Style, about 1500 BC, are covered with octopuses whose arms wrap all the way around the vessel, as if it were underwater.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Mask of Agamemnon, about 1550 to 1500 BC, gold. National Archaeological Museum, Athens.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Mask of Agamemnon. A face beaten from a thin sheet of gold: closed eyes, a long straight nose, a thin mouth, a neat beard and mustache drawn with fine lines, and ears sticking out at the sides. It covered the face of a man buried in a shaft grave at Mycenae. The flat, symmetrical design and the closed eyes give it a solemn calm. Heinrich Schliemann found it in 1876. Most experts accept it as genuine, though a few have questioned whether it was altered.
Minoan Crete built palaces like Knossos and painted lively sea creatures; Mycenae is known for walls of huge stones and gold burial masks.

Why are Mycenaean walls called "Cyclopean"? Their blocks are so enormous that later Greeks thought only the one-eyed giants of myth, the Cyclopes, could have lifted them. The Lion Gate at Mycenae, about 1250 BC, has two great lions carved in a triangle of stone above the lintel, over the entrance to the citadel.

blocks.title: Check the name
blocks.q: Schliemann telegraphed that he had "gazed on the face of Agamemnon." The mask dates to about 1550 to 1500 BC. The legendary Trojan War, if it happened, is placed around 1250 to 1180 BC. What follows?
steps: The mask is about 300 years older than the Trojan War of legend.
So it cannot be the face of a king who fought at Troy.
The name "Mask of Agamemnon" is a nickname from its finder, not an identification.
blocks.a: The mask is centuries too old to be Agamemnon's.

blocks.html: Thinking the Mask of Agamemnon belonged to Agamemnon. It is older than the Trojan War of legend; the name came from its finder, Heinrich Schliemann. Check the date of a work against the story attached to it.

blocks.html: Greek potters, above all in Athens, made vases for wine, water and oil and painted them with scenes from myth and daily life. Painted pottery survives far better than Greek wall painting, so vases are our best view of Greek painting. There are two main techniques.

items: Black-figure (in Athens, about 620 to 500 BC): figures are painted in a slip (liquid clay) that turns black in the firing, on the orange clay. Details are scratched through the black with a sharp tool, so the orange shows in thin lines.

Red-figure (invented in Athens about 530 BC): the reverse. The background is painted black and the figures are left the orange color of the clay. Details are painted on with a brush, so lines can be fine, flowing and varied.

blocks.html: Black-figure: black figures on orange clay, with scratched details. Red-figure, from about 530 BC: orange figures on a black background, with brushed details.

How does one slip turn black while the clay stays orange? The firing ran in three stages. First, with plenty of air, everything turned red. Then the potter cut off the air and added damp fuel, and everything turned black. Finally air came back in: the coarse clay turned red again, but the fine, sealed slip stayed black.

blocks.name: ar-artwork

hotspots.label: Black figures
hotspots.text: The heroes are painted in black slip on the orange clay.

hotspots.label: Scratched details
hotspots.text: Fine lines of the cloaks and armor are incised through the black.

hotspots.label: The spears
hotspots.text: Spear lines lead down to the game board between them.

blocks.cap: Exekias, Achilles and Ajax Playing a Game, about 540 to 530 BC, black-figure amphora. Vatican Museums.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Exekias's amphora. Two heroes of the Trojan War, Achilles and Ajax, lean over a low block, playing a board game between battles; painted words even give their throws. Their spears and backs form a triangle that points down to the game, the still center of the picture. Cloaks are covered in tiny incised patterns, a show of skill. Exekias signed this vase as both potter and painter.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Berlin Painter, amphora with a singer playing the kithara, about 490 BC, red-figure. The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Berlin Painter. A young man in a long robe sings, his head tipped back, playing a large lyre called a kithara. He is alone on the glossy black, with no ground line or frame, so he seems to float. The painter is unknown by name; a scholar named him in 1911 after a vase now in Berlin, and recognizes his hand by his style.

blocks.name: ar-compare
blocks.cap: Black-figure (A) and red-figure (B).

blocks.title: Which technique?
blocks.q: On a vase, a robe's folds are drawn in thin, flowing dark lines inside an orange figure, and the space around the figure is black. Which technique is it?
steps: The figure is orange: the clay color was left.
The background is black.
Orange figures on black, with brushed lines: red-figure.
blocks.a: Red-figure.

blocks.html: Mixing up the two. Ask one question: what color are the figures? Black figures on an orange ground are black-figure; orange figures on a black ground are red-figure.

blocks.html: A Greek temple is built of standard parts: a stepped platform, rows of columns, and above them the entablature (the horizontal beams) and a triangular pediment at each end. The way these parts are designed and proportioned is called an order. Greek architecture has three.

head: Order
Capital
Base
Example
blocks.cap: The three orders.

blocks.name: ar-arch
blocks.cap: Doric, Ionic and Corinthian columns.

blocks.html: Doric capitals are plain cushions and the columns have no base; Ionic capitals have scrolls; Corinthian capitals have acanthus leaves.

The orders are more than decoration. Each has a set of proportions and parts that go together, like a family resemblance: Doric is heavy and plain, Ionic is lighter, and Corinthian is the most ornate. Romans and later Renaissance architects used them as a shared language, which is why you can still find all three on banks, courthouses and museums today.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Acropolis of Athens, with the Doric Parthenon at the top.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Erechtheion, an Ionic temple on the Acropolis, about 421 to 406 BC.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Erechtheion. Next to the Parthenon stands a smaller, irregular temple in the Ionic order, with slim columns and scroll capitals on its other porches. On the south porch, seen here, six draped maidens, the caryatids, take the place of columns and carry the roof on their heads. It is the Ionic style's lightness taken to its limit.

blocks.title: Name the order
blocks.q: A column has no base, and its top is a plain round cushion under a flat square slab. Which order?
steps: Scrolls would mean Ionic; leaves would mean Corinthian.
A plain cushion and no base: Doric.
blocks.a: Doric.

blocks.html: Mixing up Ionic and Corinthian. Both are slender with bases. Look only at the capital: scrolls are Ionic; leaves are Corinthian. A memory trick: Ionic has "eyes" (two scrolls); Corinthian is crowded with leaves.

blocks.html: In the 400s BC, Athens led an alliance of Greek cities and grew rich. Under the statesman Pericles, Athenians rebuilt the temples on their Acropolis, the rocky hill above the city, which had been burned by a Persian army in 480 BC. The greatest of the new temples was the Parthenon, built from 447 to 432 BC for Athena, the city's goddess.

The architects were Iktinos and Kallikrates; the sculptor Phidias oversaw the sculpture and made the huge statue of Athena that stood inside, covered in gold and ivory (now lost). The temple is Doric, with 8 columns across each end and 17 down each side, built of white marble from Mount Pentelikon nearby. Unusually, it also had a continuous carved frieze, an Ionic feature, running around the inner building.
The Parthenon (447 to 432 BC) is a Doric marble temple to Athena on the Acropolis of Athens, designed by Iktinos and Kallikrates, with sculpture overseen by Phidias.

The Parthenon looks perfectly straight because it is not. Its floor rises in a gentle curve toward the middle of each side. Its columns swell slightly as they rise (entasis) and lean a little inward. The corner columns are a bit thicker. These refinements are tiny: the floor rises only about 6 centimeters along the side. Many think they correct optical illusions, such as a long straight line seeming to sag; they also give the building a living, springy look.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Acropolis, Athens, with the Parthenon (447 to 432 BC) under restoration.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Parthenon. From the city below, the temple sits on the highest point of the rock, a long horizontal of columns and beams against the sky. Up close the order is strict: identical units of column and space repeat all the way around. The marble was once brightly painted on its sculpture and moldings. Its history is long: it became a church, then a mosque, and in 1687, when the Ottomans were using it to store gunpowder during a Venetian siege, a cannonball set off an explosion that blew out its center.
Much of the surviving sculpture was removed between 1801 and 1812 by agents of Lord Elgin, and much of it is now in the British Museum. The rest is in the Acropolis Museum in Athens.

blocks.title: Spot the refinement
blocks.q: A careful survey finds that the Parthenon's columns are not exactly vertical. Which way do they lean, and why might the builders have done it?
steps: They lean slightly inward, toward the center of the building.
Perfectly vertical columns on a large building can seem to lean outward.
The inward lean makes the temple look stable and also braces it.
blocks.a: Slightly inward, to look (and be) more stable.

blocks.html: Thinking the Parthenon is built of perfectly straight lines. Its floor curves upward and its columns swell and lean slightly; these refinements make it look straight. Check: "looks straight" and "is straight" are different claims.

blocks.html: Greek sculpture changed more in two centuries than Egyptian sculpture did in two thousand years. In the Archaic period (about 600 to 480 BC), figures stand stiff and symmetrical, facing straight ahead, with a fixed smile (the "Archaic smile"). In the Early Classical period (about 480 to 450 BC) the smile is gone; figures look calm and serious, and poses loosen. In the High Classical period that followed, figures move and stand naturally.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Peplos Kore, about 530 BC, marble with traces of paint. Acropolis Museum, Athens.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Peplos Kore. A kore is a statue of a young woman, often set up as an offering in a sanctuary. She stands straight, frontal and nearly symmetrical. Her right arm hangs at her side with the hand closed; the left forearm, now lost, once reached forward, perhaps with an offering or, some scholars think, a bow, which would make her the goddess Artemis. Her braids fall over her shoulders, and her lips turn up in the Archaic smile. Her heavy dress hangs straight like a column. Traces of paint show she was once brightly colored: a patterned dress, colored hair, eyes and lips.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Charioteer of Delphi, about 475 BC, bronze. Delphi Archaeological Museum.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Charioteer of Delphi. Fifty years later, the change is plain. The young driver stands calm and grave, with no smile. The long robe still falls in column-like folds, but the upper body turns slightly and the folds at the waist and shoulders vary, as real cloth does. His inlaid eyes and copper lips and eyelashes make him startlingly lifelike. A ruler of Gela in Sicily dedicated the statue for a chariot victory at the Pythian Games.
Greek sculpture moved from the stiff, smiling figures of the Archaic period to the calm, natural figures of the Classical, like the bronze Charioteer of Delphi.

Why did the change happen? Sculptors studied how bodies stand and move and how cloth falls, and patrons, especially in competing city-states and sanctuaries, wanted lifelike images of gods, victors and offerings. Bronze helped: hollow-cast bronze is light and strong, so arms could stretch out without breaking, which stone cannot easily do.

blocks.title: Archaic or Classical?
blocks.q: A marble maiden stands stiffly, facing front, with a small fixed smile and braids over her shoulders. Which period?
steps: Stiff, frontal and symmetrical.
The fixed "Archaic smile".
These are Archaic traits.
blocks.a: Archaic (about 600 to 480 BC).

blocks.html: Thinking Greek statues were always white marble. They were painted in bright colors: skin, hair, eyes, clothing patterns. Most of the paint has worn away, but scientists find traces with ultraviolet light and microscopes. Check: is the white we see the artist's choice, or 2,500 years of weather?

blocks.html: In the Classical period, Greek sculptors found a way to make a standing figure look relaxed and alive. It is called contrapposto, Italian for "counterpose." The figure puts its weight on one leg. That leg is straight; the other bends at the knee. The hip above the weight-bearing leg rises, and the shoulders tilt the other way, so the body curves in a gentle S.
Contrapposto: weight on one leg, the other relaxed, hips and shoulders tilting in opposite directions. The Hellenistic age after 323 BC added drama, motion and feeling.

Stand up and try it. Put all your weight on your right leg and relax the left. Your right hip rises, and to keep your balance your shoulders tilt the other way. That is how people really stand when they are at ease. A figure carved this way looks as if it could shift and walk; a figure with weight on both feet looks frozen.

blocks.name: ar-artwork

hotspots.label: A bent knee
hotspots.text: Each maiden rests her weight on one leg and bends the other; the cloth over the bent knee pulls tight.

hotspots.label: The other side
hotspots.text: The maidens on the far side bend the opposite knee, so the porch is symmetrical.

hotspots.label: The load
hotspots.text: Each carries the roof on her head, with a cushion-like capital.

blocks.cap: The caryatids of the Erechtheion, about 421 to 406 BC. The originals are in the Acropolis Museum and the British Museum; these are copies.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The caryatids. Six maidens in long, heavy robes hold up the roof of the porch. Each stands in contrapposto: one leg straight as a column, the other bent, its knee pressing forward through the cloth. On the straight leg the robe falls in vertical folds like fluting; over the bent leg it curves and pulls. The pose turns a column into a person standing at ease, and the paired poses on the two sides keep the porch balanced.

After Alexander the Great died in 323 BC, his generals divided his empire, and Greek culture spread from Egypt to Afghanistan. Art historians call the next three centuries the Hellenistic age. Its sculptors wanted drama: twisting bodies, strong feeling, wind and motion. The most famous example is the Winged Victory of Samothrace (about 200 to 190 BC), now in the Louvre: a winged goddess landing on the prow of a stone warship, her robes whipped back by the sea wind. (We describe it here without a picture.)

blocks.title: Find the weight
blocks.q: A statue's left hip is higher than its right, and its right shoulder is higher than its left. Which leg carries the weight?
steps: The hip rises over the leg that carries the weight.
The left hip is higher.
So the weight is on the left leg, and the right leg is relaxed.
blocks.a: The left leg.

blocks.html: Thinking contrapposto only means a bent knee. It is the whole body's shift of weight: one hip up, the opposite shoulder up. Check the hips and shoulders, not only the knees.

blocks.html: Romans admired Greek temples and borrowed the orders, but their great invention was a new way to enclose space. They used three tools together: the round arch, the vault (an arch extended into a tunnel, or two tunnels crossing, called a groin vault) and concrete, made of lime, volcanic ash called pozzolana, water and chunks of stone or brick. Roman concrete could be poured into wooden forms and even hardened underwater.

blocks.name: ar-arch
blocks.cap: A barrel vault, a groin vault and (later, in Gothic churches) a ribbed vault.

blocks.html: With the round arch, the vault and concrete, Romans built aqueducts like the Pont du Gard, the Colosseum and the domed Pantheon: big interior spaces the Greeks never built.

An arch works because its wedge-shaped stones push against each other, turning the weight above into a sideways push that runs down to the supports. Stone is very strong when squeezed, so an arch can span far more than a flat stone beam, which would crack under its own weight.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Pont du Gard, near Nîmes, France, about AD 40 to 60.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Pont du Gard. Three tiers of arches carry a water channel across the Gardon River, about 49 meters above the riverbed. The bottom two tiers have big arches; the top tier has many small ones under the channel. It is built of huge stones fitted without mortar. Its beauty comes from repetition and proportion: arch after arch, the rhythm of a structure that does one job well.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Colosseum (Flavian Amphitheater), Rome, AD 70 to 80.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The dome of the Pantheon, Rome, about AD 113 to 125, seen from below.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Pantheon. Look up. The dome is a perfect hemisphere of concrete, 43 meters across, and the floor is the same distance below its top, so a giant ball would fit inside. Five rings of sunken panels (coffers) shrink toward the top, lightening the dome and leading the eye to the oculus, an open circle about 9 meters wide. It is the only window: a disk of sunlight moves across the walls through the day, and rain falls through to drains in the floor. The builders made the concrete lighter as it rose, ending with pumice, a light volcanic stone, near the top. After nearly 1,900 years it is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.

blocks.title: Read the inscription
blocks.q: The Pantheon's porch says, in Latin, "Marcus Agrippa made this." Agrippa died in 12 BC. Who built the building we see?
steps: Agrippa built an earlier temple on the site, which burned.
The present building was built under the emperor Hadrian, about AD 113 to 125.
Hadrian kept Agrippa's name on the new porch.
blocks.a: Hadrian; the inscription honors Agrippa's earlier temple.

blocks.html: Thinking the Romans only copied Greek temples. Concrete, arches and vaults let them build interior spaces the Greeks never did: domes, vaulted halls, markets and amphitheaters. Check: a Greek temple is mostly an outside; the Pantheon is mostly an inside.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive, analyze and interpret artistic work)

blocks.html: Romans wanted portraits that looked like real people. In the late Republic (the 100s and 1st century BC), many marble portrait heads of older men show every wrinkle, sag and bony cheek. This style is called verism, from the Latin for "true." The wrinkles were a point of pride: they stood for experience, seriousness and service to the state. (Under the emperors, official portraits became smoother and more idealized.)

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Portrait of a Couple (Terentius Neo and His Wife), Pompeii, 1st century AD (before 79), fresco. National Archaeological Museum, Naples.

blocks.html: Looking closely: A couple from Pompeii. A man and a woman look straight at us, side by side, painted on the wall of their house. She holds a stylus to her lips and a folding wax tablet; he holds a scroll. Those props say "we can read and write," a sign of status. Their faces are individual, with real features: her thick, meeting eyebrows, his short beard and tanned skin. Shading on cheeks and noses makes the heads round. The house is identified as Terentius Neo's from painted notices outside it, but who the couple were is not certain.

When Mount Vesuvius erupted in AD 79, ash buried Pompeii and nearby towns, preserving hundreds of wall paintings. Many walls were painted to look like something else: colored marble, columns, windows onto distant views.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Garden Room from the Villa of Livia, near Rome, about 30 to 20 BC, fresco. National Roman Museum, Rome.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Livia's garden room. This room was half underground, a cool retreat for the wife of the emperor Augustus. All four walls were painted as a garden: a low fence, then a lawn, then trees and bushes heavy with fruit and flowers, with birds flying among them under a blue sky. The near plants are sharp; the far ones are hazier and bluer. You seem to stand in an open garden rather than in a closed room.
Republican portraits show age and wrinkles (verism); Roman wall paintings, at Pompeii and in Livia's villa, open walls into gardens and views with shading and depth.

How did the painters suggest depth? Overlapping (near plants in front of far ones), shading (light and dark on round forms) and haze (distant things paler and bluer, which painters later called atmospheric perspective). They had no single mathematical system like the one the Renaissance invented, but they used the eye's cues well.

blocks.title: Why show wrinkles?
blocks.q: A Roman senator of about 60 BC orders a portrait that shows him old, wrinkled and bony-cheeked. Why would he want that?
steps: In Republican Rome, public life honored age, experience and duty.
Wrinkles showed a life of hard service.
So an unflattering likeness was a flattering message.
blocks.a: Wrinkles stood for experience and service, values the Republic honored.

blocks.html: Thinking the Romans painted only flat walls. Their wall paintings used shading, overlapping and haze to suggest depth, centuries before the Renaissance. Check the far trees in Livia's garden: paler and bluer than the near ones.

blocks.html: For nearly three centuries, Christians in the Roman Empire met in houses and buried their dead in underground cemeteries (catacombs), where they painted simple images on the walls. In AD 313 the emperors Constantine and Licinius agreed, in what is called the Edict of Milan, to tolerate Christianity. Constantine then paid for large churches. The question was what a church should look like.

Temples would not do: a Roman temple was a house for a god's statue, with sacrifices outside, and it held few people. Builders chose instead the basilica, a Roman public hall used for law courts and business. A basilica is a long hall with a tall central nave, lower aisles on each side behind rows of columns, windows high in the nave walls (the clerestory), and a rounded apse at one end, where a judge had once sat. In a church, the altar stood before the apse. An entrance porch, the narthex, sat at the other end, and some large churches added a cross-arm, the transept.

blocks.name: ar-arch
blocks.cap: The plan of a basilica.

blocks.html: After AD 313, Christians built basilicas, long halls with a nave, aisles and an apse, borrowed from Roman public buildings.

The basilica fit what churches needed: room for a large congregation, a strong line from the door to the altar, and light from the clerestory. Its long axis turns a building into a path, from the entrance toward the apse. Old St. Peter's in Rome, begun under Constantine in the 320s, was a huge basilica; it stood until it was replaced in the 1500s. Santa Sabina in Rome (422 to 432) still stands much as it was built.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Christ as the Good Shepherd, Mausoleum of Galla Placidia, Ravenna, about AD 425 to 450, mosaic.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Good Shepherd. Above a doorway in a small cross-shaped chapel in Ravenna, a young, beardless shepherd sits among rocks and plants, with sheep around him, three on each side. He wears a gold robe with a purple mantle, the colors of an emperor, and holds a tall cross like a shepherd's staff. The scene still has Roman roots: a landscape, shading on the robe, sheep turning in space. But the gold halo and the cross make it a Christian image of Christ as protector. The glass tesserae glow against a deep blue sky.

blocks.title: Read the plan
blocks.q: You walk into a church through a porch, down a long central space with columns on both sides, toward a curved end wall. Name the parts in order.
steps: The entrance porch: the narthex.
The tall central space: the nave, with aisles beyond the columns.
The curved end: the apse.
blocks.a: Narthex, nave (with aisles), apse.

blocks.html: Thinking a basilica is a religious building in origin. The Romans built basilicas first as law courts and meeting halls; Christians adopted the plan. Today the word is also a title the Catholic Church gives to certain important churches, which is a different use.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive, analyze and interpret artistic work)

blocks.html: The Roman Empire split into a western half, which fell apart in the 400s, and an eastern half ruled from Constantinople, which lasted another thousand years. Historians call that eastern empire Byzantine. In 540 the Byzantine emperor Justinian won back Ravenna in northern Italy, and in 547 the church of San Vitale there was consecrated, its apse covered in some of the finest mosaics that survive.

A mosaic is made of tesserae, small cubes of colored stone and glass pressed into wet mortar. For gold, a thin leaf of gold was sealed between two layers of glass. The cubes were set at slight angles, so they catch light unevenly and glitter as you move or as candlelight flickers.

blocks.name: ar-artwork

hotspots.label: The crown
hotspots.text: Jeweled, with hanging pearls.

hotspots.label: The halo
hotspots.text: A sign of the emperor's sacred role.

hotspots.label: The eyes
hotspots.text: Large, dark and staring straight out.

hotspots.label: The brooch
hotspots.text: A large jeweled clasp holds the purple cloak.

hotspots.label: Imperial purple
hotspots.text: Purple dye was costly and reserved for the emperor.

hotspots.label: The gold ground
hotspots.text: Gold glass tesserae, set at angles so they glitter.

blocks.cap: Emperor Justinian, from the mosaic of Justinian and His Attendants, San Vitale, Ravenna, about AD 547.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Justinian and Theodora. On one wall of the apse, Justinian stands at the center of a row of churchmen, officials and soldiers, holding a golden dish of bread for the service; on the opposite wall, the empress Theodora carries a gold chalice, with her ladies. The figures stand in a shallow line, facing us, their feet barely touching the ground, which seems to tilt up beneath them. Their bodies are hidden by long robes that fall in straight lines, so they look tall and weightless. The faces are individual, with large eyes, but the setting is gold, not a room. Neither ruler is known to have visited Ravenna: the mosaics place them there forever, in image.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Empress Theodora, from the mosaic of Theodora and Her Attendants, San Vitale, about AD 547.

blocks.html: At San Vitale in Ravenna (about AD 547), glittering mosaics of glass and stone show the emperor Justinian and the empress Theodora with their courts, as if taking part in the service forever.

Why make figures flat and gold-bound? The goal was not to show a moment in a real room but a lasting, holy order: emperor and empress as part of the worship at the altar, above time. Gold, frontal poses and repetition say "eternal," much as a halo does.

blocks.title: What kind of space?
blocks.q: Compare the Good Shepherd mosaic (about 425 to 450) with the Justinian panel (about 547). Which shows deeper space?
steps: The Good Shepherd sits in a landscape with rocks, plants and a sky, and the sheep turn in space.
The Justinian panel shows a row of standing figures against flat gold, with almost no ground.
So the earlier mosaic is deeper; Byzantine art moved toward flatness on purpose.
blocks.a: The earlier Good Shepherd mosaic.

blocks.name: ar-compare
blocks.cap: Early Christian (A) and Byzantine (B) mosaics in Ravenna.

blocks.html: Expecting the figures to look solid. Byzantine mosaics flatten figures and float them on gold to show a heavenly, timeless world. Check: is flatness a lack of skill, or a choice? The same workshops could model forms when they wanted to.

blocks.html: In 532, riots in Constantinople burned the city's cathedral. Justinian rebuilt it at once, on a scale no one had tried. He chose two scholars of mathematics and engineering, Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, as architects. The new church of Hagia Sophia, Greek for "Holy Wisdom," was finished in about five years, from 532 to 537.

The challenge was to put a round dome over a square space. Romans had built domes on round walls, like the Pantheon's. Here, four huge arches stand on four piers around a square, and between the arches curved triangles of masonry, called pendentives, rise and lean inward until they form a ring. The dome, about 31 meters across, sits on that ring. Half-domes at the east and west extend the space into a long oval.

blocks.name: ar-arch
blocks.cap: A dome on pendentives over a square plan.

blocks.html: Hagia Sophia (AD 532 to 537), by Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, set a huge dome on pendentives over a square plan in Constantinople.

Pendentives solve a geometry problem. A circle sits inside a square, touching it only at four points; the corners are left open. Each pendentive is a piece of a larger sphere that fills one corner and carries the dome's weight down to a pier. Around the dome's base is a ring of 40 windows, so the dome seems to float on light. That floating was fragile: earthquakes cracked it, and in 558 the dome fell. It was rebuilt by 562, steeper and taller.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Hagia Sophia, Istanbul, AD 532 to 537, in an engraving of 1877. The minarets were added after 1453.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Hagia Sophia. From outside, a great low dome rises over a mass of half-domes and buttresses that step down around it like a hillside. Inside, the space opens upward: arches, half-domes and the dome itself rise one above another, and light pours in through the windows at the dome's base. Its walls were sheathed in colored marble and its vaults in gold mosaic. In 1453 the Ottoman Turks captured Constantinople, and the church became a mosque, with a mihrab, a minbar and, over time, four minarets. It was a museum from 1934 and is used as a mosque again today, open to visitors.

blocks.title: How does a round dome sit on a square?
blocks.q: Explain in three steps how Hagia Sophia's dome rests on four piers.
steps: Four great arches span the four sides of the square, resting on four piers at the corners.
Between each pair of arches, a curved triangle of masonry (a pendentive) fills the corner and leans inward.
The four pendentives meet in a circle at the top, and the dome sits on that circle.
blocks.a: Arches on piers, pendentives in the corners, and the dome on the ring they make.

blocks.html: Thinking the minarets are part of the original church. They were added after 1453, when it became a mosque. Check the dates of each part of a building, not just its founding date.

blocks.cap: Hagia Sophia was built during the Byzantine period.

blocks.html: An icon (Greek eikōn, "image") is a holy image, usually painted on a wooden panel, of Christ, the Virgin Mary or a saint. In the Orthodox churches of the Byzantine world and later of Russia, Greece and the Balkans, icons are honored with candles, bows and prayer; the honor is understood to pass to the person shown, not the wood and paint.

Icons were painted in egg tempera on a wooden panel coated with gesso (a smooth white ground of chalk or gypsum and glue), often with gold leaf behind the figures. Painters worked from dark to light, laying thin layers of brighter color over a darker base to build up faces.
An icon is a holy image painted on wood, often in egg tempera with gold. Icons follow set types, so faces and poses repeat across centuries.

Why would painters copy old types instead of inventing? An icon was meant to be a true image of a holy person, faithful to images believed to go back to early times. Repeating the type was a sign of faithfulness. Within the type, painters still showed great skill in the drawing, the color and the feeling of a face.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Theotokos of Vladimir, about 1130, tempera on wood, painted in Constantinople. State Tretyakov Gallery, Moscow.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Virgin of Vladimir. Mary holds the Christ Child, who presses his cheek against hers and clings to her. This type is called the Eleousa, "of tenderness." Her face is long and grave, with a small mouth, a long nose and large, sad eyes that look past the child toward us, as if she knows his future. The dark robes are simple shapes; the child's robe glints with gold lines. The faces are the original 12th-century paint; other parts were repainted over the centuries. Sent from Constantinople to Kiev in the 1130s, the icon was taken to Vladimir in 1155 and to Moscow in 1395, and it became one of the most honored images in Russia.

Icons were not always accepted. From about 726 to 787, and again from 815 to 843, Byzantine emperors banned religious images, a period called Iconoclasm ("image-breaking"), and many were destroyed. In 843 icons were restored for good, which is one reason so few earlier icons survive.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Duccio, Maestà, 1308 to 1311, Siena. Italian painting drew on Byzantine icons.

blocks.title: Icon or Renaissance portrait?
blocks.q: A panel shows a holy woman with a long, solemn face, against a gold background, in a pose found on hundreds of other panels. What tradition is it, and why the repetition?
steps: Gold ground, a holy subject and a fixed type are features of icons.
The pose repeats because icons follow set types handed down over centuries.
The aim is faithfulness to a holy image, not a new likeness.
blocks.a: An icon; it repeats a traditional type on purpose.

blocks.html: Judging icons as failed realism. Their makers aimed at sameness and spiritual presence, not likeness. Check what the maker was trying to do before calling something a failure.
Italian painters of the 1200s learned from icons; Duccio's Maestà for Siena keeps the gold and the long faces. You will see how Giotto broke away.

blocks.html: Islam began in Arabia in the early 600s, and within a century Muslim rulers governed lands from Spain to Central Asia. The central building of Islam is the mosque (from Arabic masjid, "place of prostration"), where Muslims pray together, especially at noon on Fridays. Muslims pray facing Mecca, so every mosque is laid out around that direction.

blocks.name: ar-arch
blocks.cap: The plan of a courtyard mosque.

items: The qibla wall is the wall that faces Mecca; worshipers line up facing it.
The mihrab is a niche in the qibla wall that marks the direction of prayer.
The minbar is a stepped pulpit beside the mihrab, from which the Friday sermon is given.
The prayer hall is the covered space in front of the qibla wall; many mosques also have a courtyard with water for washing before prayer.
A minaret is a tower from which the call to prayer was given.

blocks.html: A mosque's prayer hall faces Mecca: the qibla wall holds the mihrab niche, the minbar is the pulpit, and a minaret is a tower for the call to prayer. Plans vary widely.

Unlike a church, a mosque does not need a long axis toward an altar. What it needs is a wide wall facing Mecca, so that rows of worshipers can stand side by side. That is why many early mosques are wider than they are deep, with rows of columns holding up a flat roof: a hypostyle hall, from the Greek for "under columns."

What it is

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Dome of the Rock, Jerusalem, completed AD 691 to 692.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Dome of the Rock. The Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik built it on the great platform in Jerusalem that Muslims call the Noble Sanctuary and Jews call the Temple Mount. It is not a mosque but a shrine, built around a sacred rock. An octagon of walls holds two rings of columns, so visitors can walk around the rock beneath a high, gilded dome. Long inscriptions in angular Arabic script, dated to the year 72 of the Islamic calendar (AD 691 to 692), run around the inside; they are among the earliest surviving Islamic inscriptions. The blue tiles outside are later, from the 1500s, and the gold dome has been restored many times.

blocks.title: Find the direction
blocks.q: You enter a mosque you have never seen. How can you tell which way Mecca is?
steps: Look for the niche in one wall: the mihrab.
The wall with the mihrab is the qibla wall, and it faces Mecca.
The minbar, a stepped pulpit, usually stands beside it.
blocks.a: The mihrab in the qibla wall shows the direction of Mecca.

blocks.html: Thinking every mosque has a dome and four minarets. Plans vary widely: hypostyle halls of columns, courtyards with iwans, central domes; some mosques have one minaret or none. Check the plan before you name the style.
