blocks.html: Islamic art is famous for three kinds of ornament, often used together on one surface.

items: Geometric pattern: stars, polygons and interlacing bands built with a compass and a straightedge, repeating in every direction.
Arabesque: flowing, branching vines and leaves that curl and split rhythmically and could go on forever.

Calligraphy: beautiful writing, especially of the words of the Qur'an. It is the most honored art in the Islamic world. Early scripts such as Kufic are angular and stately; later rounded scripts such as naskh are easier to read and became the usual book hand.

blocks.name: ar-pattern
blocks.cap: An eight-pointed star pattern, built from squares turned against each other.

blocks.html: Islamic ornament combines geometric pattern, arabesque (flowing vine scrolls) and calligraphy, the most honored art.

Why so much pattern? In religious settings, such as mosques and copies of the Qur'an, Muslim tradition generally avoided images of people and animals, so ornament carried the beauty and meaning. Patterns that repeat without end were seen by many as a fitting sign of an infinite God. And the Qur'an is the word of God in Arabic, so writing it beautifully was a way of honoring it.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Mosque lamp bearing the name of Sultan al-Malik al-Nasir, Egypt or Syria, about 1340, enameled and gilded glass. The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

blocks.html: Looking closely: A mosque lamp. Tall Arabic letters in blue enamel march around the lamp's body and neck, their upright strokes making a strong rhythm. Between them, smaller panels hold vine scrolls and flowers. The words name the sultan who paid for it. Lamps like this hung from chains by their small handles, with an oil lamp inside, so the glass glowed and the letters stood out in the light. Many such lamps carry the Qur'an's Verse of Light, which compares God's light to a lamp in a niche.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Court of the Lions, Alhambra, Granada, 1370s.

blocks.html: At the Alhambra in Spain, walls are covered in carved plaster: arabesques, geometric panels and bands of writing, including poems praising the palace. You will visit it in Córdoba and the Alhambra.

blocks.title: Name the ornament
blocks.q: A tile shows an eight-pointed star made of two overlapping squares, surrounded by interlocking shapes that repeat across the wall. Which kind of ornament is it?
steps: Vine scrolls would be arabesque; letters would be calligraphy.
Stars and polygons that repeat are geometric pattern.
blocks.a: Geometric pattern.

blocks.html: Thinking Islamic art has no images of people at all. Religious settings generally avoid them, but palaces, illustrated books, ceramics and metalwork often show figures: princes, hunters, musicians, scenes from poems. Check the setting: mosque or palace, Qur'an or book of poems?

blocks.html: Muslim armies crossed from North Africa into Spain in 711, and for nearly eight centuries Muslim rulers governed much of the Iberian Peninsula, which they called al-Andalus. Two of its buildings are among the most beautiful in the world: a mosque in Córdoba and a palace in Granada.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The prayer hall of the Great Mosque of Córdoba, begun about 785 and enlarged until about 987. A photograph of about 1900.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Great Mosque of Córdoba. The emir Abd al-Rahman I, a prince of the Umayyad family from Syria, began the mosque about 785. Later rulers enlarged it again and again, until it had hundreds of columns, many reused from Roman and Visigothic buildings. The columns were short, so the builders stacked a second tier of arches on top of the first to raise the roof: lower horseshoe arches and upper round ones. The arch stones alternate red brick and pale stone, so stripes march off in every direction like the trees of a forest. In the 960s the caliph al-Hakam II added a glittering mihrab decorated with mosaics. After Christian armies took Córdoba in 1236, the mosque became a cathedral, and in 1523 a Renaissance church was built in its middle.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Court of the Lions, Alhambra, Granada, 1370s, for Sultan Muhammad V.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Court of the Lions. The Alhambra ("the red one," for the color of its walls) is a hilltop fortress and palace of the Nasrid sultans, the last Muslim rulers in Spain, mostly built in the 1300s. In the Court of the Lions, a garden courtyard is ringed by 124 slender marble columns, single and paired, carrying arches of carved plaster as fine as lace. At the center, water spouts from a basin carried by twelve stone lions and runs in channels toward the halls on each side. In the rooms beside it, ceilings are built of muqarnas: thousands of small niches stacked in tiers, like honeycomb or stalactites. Poems by the court poet Ibn Zamrak are carved into the walls.
The Great Mosque of Córdoba (begun about 785) has rows of striped double arches; the Alhambra palaces of Granada (mostly 1300s) have carved plaster, water and muqarnas ceilings.

Why do the Alhambra's rooms feel weightless? The structure is plain brick and timber; the carved plaster and tile are a skin laid over it. Light, water and endlessly repeating pattern dissolve the walls. Visitors sense a garden of paradise, an idea inscriptions on the walls make explicit.

blocks.title: Mosque or palace?
blocks.q: A visitor calls the Alhambra "the great mosque of Granada." Correct the claim.
steps: The Alhambra is a fortress and a complex of palaces for the Nasrid sultans and their court.
It had small prayer rooms, but it was a royal residence, not a mosque.
The great mosque in al-Andalus is the one at Córdoba.
blocks.a: It is a palace and fortress, not a mosque.

blocks.html: Thinking the Alhambra is a mosque. It is a palace and fortress of the Nasrid rulers. Check a building's function before you name its type.

blocks.html: In Europe, art history often centers on painting and sculpture. In the Islamic world, some of the most prized arts were what Europeans called "decorative": carpets and textiles, metalwork, glass, ceramics and books. Kings paid as much for a great carpet or a finely copied manuscript as any European prince paid for an altarpiece.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Ardabil Carpet, Safavid Iran, 1539 to 1540, wool pile on silk. Victoria and Albert Museum, London.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Ardabil Carpet. It is about 10.5 by 5.3 meters, one of a pair made under Shah Tahmasp for the shrine of Shaykh Safi al-Din at Ardabil, the ancestor of the Safavid kings. A pointed golden medallion sits at the center of a deep blue field filled with flowers and curling stems. Two lamps of unequal size hang from it toward the ends, and a quarter of the medallion repeats in each corner, as if the design continued under the borders. A woven panel at one end gives a line of verse, the date 946 in the Islamic calendar (1539 to 1540), and the name of Maqsud of Kashan, "servant of the court." It has about 340 knots in every square inch, some 26 million in all. Its twin, cut down to repair it in the 1800s, is in the Los Angeles County Museum of Art.
Luxury arts carried Islamic design across the world: knotted carpets like the Ardabil carpet (1539 to 1540), enameled glass mosque lamps and illustrated manuscripts.

A knotted carpet is a picture made one knot at a time. Weavers tie a short length of colored wool around threads of the foundation, row after row, and beat each row down. Every knot is one dot of color, like a pixel. More knots per inch means finer detail, and many more months of work.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: A Mamluk mosque lamp, about 1340, enameled and gilded glass.

blocks.html: Glassmakers in Mamluk Egypt and Syria blew lamps like this one and painted them with colored enamel and gold, then fired them again to fuse the colors. Hundreds hung in the mosques and schools of Cairo.

Books were treasured too. Persian painters made small, brilliant paintings called miniatures for copies of poems such as the Shahnameh (Book of Kings), with flat bright colors, fine detail and gold. Calligraphers, painters, gilders and binders worked together in royal workshops.

blocks.title: Count the knots
blocks.q: A carpet has 300 knots in every square inch. A small section is 10 inches by 10 inches. How many knots is that?
steps: 10 × 10 = 100 square inches.
Every one tied by hand.
blocks.a: 30,000 knots.

blocks.html: Thinking these were minor crafts. In the Islamic world, textiles, metalwork, glass and books were among the most prized arts, made by named masters for kings and shrines. Check how the people who made and used a work valued it.

blocks.cap: Sort the works by medium.

blocks.html: Before printing, every book in Europe was copied by hand, most of them by monks and nuns in a monastery's writing room, the scriptorium. Pages were made of vellum or parchment, calfskin or sheepskin soaked, scraped and stretched thin. A decorated book is called an illuminated manuscript, from the Latin for "lit up," because gold and bright colors seem to glow on the page.

On the islands of Britain and Ireland, monks of the 600s to 800s created a style called Insular (from Latin insula, "island"). It mixed the interlace and spirals of Celtic and Anglo-Saxon metalwork with Mediterranean book design. Two masterpieces stand out.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: A carpet page from the Lindisfarne Gospels, about 715 to 720. British Library, London.

blocks.html: Looking closely: A Lindisfarne carpet page. A whole page with no words, covered edge to edge like a rug, so it is called a carpet page. A cross in red, blue and gold stands out against a dense field of interlace: ribbons, and the twisting bodies of birds and beasts, that weave over and under each other without a break. It was laid out with compass and ruler and then filled by hand. A note added in the 900s says Eadfrith, bishop of Lindisfarne, wrote the book; so the book is "attributed to" him.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Chi Rho page of the Book of Kells, about 800. Trinity College Library, Dublin.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Chi Rho page. This page begins the story of Christ's birth in Matthew's Gospel. Two Greek letters, Chi (X) and Rho (P), the first letters of "Christ" in Greek, swell to fill nearly the whole page, and every stroke of them is packed with spirals, knots and tiny figures. Look closely and you find faces, angels, and animals hidden in the ornament, including cats watching mice and an otter with a fish. Where the book was made is debated: on the island of Iona, off Scotland; at Kells in Ireland, where monks fled after Viking raids; or partly at both.
Monks copied and decorated books by hand. The Lindisfarne Gospels (about 715) and the Book of Kells (about 800) fill pages with knotwork and interlace.

Why lavish so much work on a book? These were Gospel books, the words of the Christian scriptures, used on the altar and carried in processions. To their makers, the text deserved the richest frame they could make, as a reliquary honors a relic. A single book could take years and the skins of many calves.

blocks.title: Read the page
blocks.q: A full page in an Insular gospel book has a cross set in dense interlace and no text at all. What is it called, and where does it come in the book?
steps: A full page of pure ornament, like a rug: a carpet page.
In the Lindisfarne Gospels, carpet pages come before each Gospel, like a doorway.
blocks.a: A carpet page, placed before a Gospel.

blocks.html: Calling the whole Middle Ages the "Dark Ages," when nothing of value was made. Books like these are among the most intricate art ever made, and the monasteries that made them kept learning alive. Check: "dark" usually means we have fewer written records, not that people made nothing.

blocks.name: ar-map
blocks.cap: Lindisfarne and Durham in northern England; Dublin, where the Book of Kells is now.

blocks.html: Around the year 1000, Western Europe grew more settled and prosperous, and church building boomed. Huge numbers of pilgrims traveled to holy sites such as Santiago de Compostela in Spain, and churches along the way grew larger to hold them and their saints' relics. The style of about 1000 to 1150 is called Romanesque.

items: Round arches over doors, windows and arcades.
Thick walls and massive piers, because stone vaults push outward and the walls must hold them in.
Barrel vaults or groin vaults of stone, which resisted fire better than wooden roofs.
Small windows, because big openings would weaken the thick walls.
Carved portals: the semicircle over the main door (the tympanum) often showed a great scene in relief for everyone entering.

blocks.html: Romanesque churches (about 1000 to 1150) have thick walls, round arches, barrel vaults and small windows, and carved portals for pilgrims.

Why so heavy? A stone vault presses down and also pushes sideways, trying to spread the walls apart. Romanesque builders answered with mass: thick walls, few openings, heavy piers. It worked, but it kept the interiors fairly dark. The next generation would find another answer.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Basilica of Saint-Sernin, Toulouse, France, about 1080 to 1120, from the east.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Saint-Sernin. A pilgrimage church on the road to Santiago, built of red brick and pale stone. From the east end you see the building step up like a hill: small round chapels at the bottom ring the curved end of the church, then a higher curved wall, then the main roof, then a tall octagonal tower in tiers of round-arched openings. Every window and arcade is round-headed, and the walls are thick and solid. The ring of chapels let crowds walk around the east end to visit relics without disturbing services at the main altar.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The nave of Durham Cathedral, England, 1093 to 1133.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Durham's nave. Massive round piers, cut with zigzags and spirals, alternate with clustered piers down the nave, all carrying round arches. Overhead, though, are something new: stone ribs that cross the vault in an X. Durham has some of the earliest ribbed vaults in Europe, and some of its arches are slightly pointed, hints of the Gothic to come.

blocks.name: ar-arch
blocks.cap: Romanesque (A), Gothic (B) and Renaissance (C) church fronts.

blocks.title: Name the style
blocks.q: A church has a thick wall, a round-arched doorway with a carved semicircle above it, and only small round-topped windows. Which style?
steps: Round arches: not Gothic.
Thick walls and small windows: the heavy solution to the thrust of vaults.
A carved tympanum over the door.
blocks.a: Romanesque.

blocks.html: Thinking "Romanesque" means built by the Romans. It means "in the Roman manner": round arches and heavy masonry, about a thousand years after Rome. The name was invented in the 1800s. Check the date: Roman buildings end around AD 500; Romanesque ones begin around 1000.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive, analyze and interpret artistic work)

blocks.html: About 1140, Abbot Suger rebuilt the east end of the abbey church of Saint-Denis, near Paris, with a ring of chapels whose walls were mostly glass. Suger wrote that the light through colored glass lifted the mind toward God. Within a century, cathedrals all over northern France were going up in the new style, later called Gothic.
Gothic builders combined three tools, none new on its own:

items: Pointed arches, which push less sideways than round ones and can be made taller or shorter for the same width.
Ribbed vaults, a skeleton of stone ribs that carries the weight of the vault to a few points.
Flying buttresses, arms of stone outside the building that reach over the aisles to brace the high walls against the vault's outward push.

blocks.name: ar-arch
blocks.cap: A Gothic cross-section: the flying buttress braces the wall, so the clerestory can be filled with glass.

blocks.html: Gothic builders, from about 1140, combined pointed arches, ribbed vaults and flying buttresses to raise tall, thin walls filled with glass.

In a Romanesque church, the wall itself holds the vault in, so it must be thick and nearly solid. In a Gothic church, the ribs gather the vault's weight onto piers, and the flying buttresses catch its sideways push outside. The wall between the piers carries almost nothing, so it can become a window. The structure moved outside, and the inside filled with light.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Notre-Dame de Paris, begun 1163; the west front about 1200 to 1250. A photograph of about 1890 to 1900.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Notre-Dame de Paris. The west front is a great square divided in three: three pointed doorways at the bottom, a row of carved kings, a rose window at the center flanked by tall pointed windows, a light open gallery, and two square towers. Everything is balanced and firmly organized, yet the surfaces are opened up by arches and tracery. Along the sides, flying buttresses reach out like oars. A fire in 2019 destroyed the roof and spire; the cathedral was restored and reopened in December 2024.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Royal Portal, west front of Chartres Cathedral, about 1145, in an early photograph.

blocks.html: At Chartres, a fire in 1194 destroyed most of the earlier church, but its west front survived, with its tall, slender column figures of kings and queens of the Bible. The new cathedral rose behind it, mostly between 1194 and 1220, and it still has most of its medieval stained glass.

blocks.title: Romanesque or Gothic?
blocks.q: A church has tall pointed windows filling most of its walls, ribs on the vault, and arched supports outside reaching over the side aisles. Which style, and why can the walls be so thin?
steps: Pointed arches, rib vaults and flying buttresses are the Gothic trio.
The ribs bring the weight down to piers; the flying buttresses brace against the outward push.
So the walls between the piers carry little load and can be glass.
blocks.a: Gothic; the frame of piers and buttresses carries the load.

blocks.html: Thinking the Goths built Gothic churches. The Goths were a Germanic people of the 300s to 500s. The name was a later insult from Renaissance writers such as Giorgio Vasari, who thought the style barbaric compared with Roman architecture. Check the dates: about 700 years apart.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive, analyze and interpret artistic work)

blocks.html: A Gothic window is a picture made of light. Glassmakers colored molten glass with metal oxides: cobalt for blue, copper for green and red, iron or manganese for other colors. They blew it into sheets, which the glazier cut into pieces following a full-size drawing. Painters added faces, folds and lettering with a dark paint made of ground glass and iron oxide, and fired the pieces in a kiln so the paint fused to the glass. Then the pieces were fitted into H-shaped strips of lead, called cames, soldered at the joints, and the panels were set into an iron frame in the window.
Pieces of colored glass held in lead strips filled Gothic windows with light and stories; Chartres and the Sainte-Chapelle (1242 to 1248) are famous for it.

Why does stained glass glow? A painting reflects light from its surface. Stained glass transmits light: sunlight passes through the colored glass, so the color comes straight to your eye, far brighter than anything around it in a dim church. The dark lead lines make the colors look brighter still, the way a dark outline does in a cartoon.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The north rose window of Chartres Cathedral, about 1230 to 1235, with five lancet windows below.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The north rose at Chartres. A great wheel of glass about 10 meters across, set in stone tracery. From a small circle at the center, rings of shapes radiate outward like the petals of a flower: circles, then squares set on their corners, then half-circles at the rim. Each holds figures, too small to read from the floor but clear as color: deep blue grounds and red borders. Below stand five tall lancets with standing figures. The design is as strictly geometric as a snowflake.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The upper chapel of the Sainte-Chapelle, Paris, 1242 to 1248.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Sainte-Chapelle. King Louis IX of France built this chapel in his palace to hold relics he had bought, above all the Crown of Thorns. Its upper chapel is almost all window: fifteen tall windows of glass, separated only by thin stone piers, telling more than a thousand stories from the Bible. On a sunny day the walls dissolve into blue and red light. It was built very fast, between 1242 and 1248.

blocks.title: Where is the color?
blocks.q: A guide says, "the painters colored the windows with paint." Correct it.
steps: The main colors are in the glass itself, made by adding metal oxides to the molten glass.
Painters added only dark lines and shading with a glass-based paint, fired on.
The lead cames outline the pieces.
blocks.a: The color is in the glass; painting added only lines and shading.

blocks.html: Thinking the glass was painted all over. The color is in the glass; painters added only lines and shading in a dark glass paint, fired in a kiln. Check by looking at a broken piece: the color runs all the way through.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive, analyze and interpret artistic work)

blocks.html: A book of hours is a prayer book for people who were not priests or monks. It held prayers for the eight "hours" of the day, prayers to the Virgin Mary, psalms, and a calendar of saints' days, month by month. In the 1300s and 1400s books of hours were the most common books in Western Europe. Wealthy owners ordered them richly painted.

The most famous is the Très Riches Heures ("very rich hours") made for Jean, Duke of Berry, a brother of the French king and a passionate collector. The painters were three brothers from the Netherlands, Paul, Herman and Jean (Johan) Limbourg. They worked on it from about 1412 until 1416, when all three brothers and the duke died, probably of the plague. Other painters completed it in the 1480s.

blocks.name: ar-artwork

hotspots.label: The duke
hotspots.text: Jean de Berry in blue with a fur hat, seated before a woven screen.

hotspots.label: Words in gold
hotspots.text: "Aproche, aproche" ("come closer"), perhaps a servant inviting guests forward.

hotspots.label: The feast
hotspots.text: Gold dishes and a table laid with food.

hotspots.label: A tapestry
hotspots.text: Behind the guests hangs a tapestry of knights in battle.

hotspots.label: The little dogs
hotspots.text: Small dogs eat from the table.

blocks.cap: The Limbourg brothers, Très Riches Heures: January, about 1412 to 1416, tempera and gold on vellum. Musée Condé, Chantilly.

blocks.html: Looking closely: January. It is New Year, when gifts were exchanged, and the duke holds a feast. He sits at the right in deep blue, his fur hat making him easy to find, while courtiers crowd in from the left in brilliant reds, greens and blues. Behind them a tapestry shows knights fighting, as if a war story were part of the decoration. Every surface is patterned: the blue cloth with gold fleurs-de-lis, the gold dishes, the striped floor. The figures are slender and elegant, and the space is shallow, like a stage. This crowded, jewel-like style of the courts around 1400 is called International Gothic.
Wealthy owners ordered prayer books with calendar pictures, like the Limbourg brothers' Très Riches Heures (about 1412 to 1416) for the Duke of Berry.

Why do prayer books show feasts and farming? The calendar pages marked the months, and each month had its labors, traditional tasks such as plowing in March or harvesting in summer. The Limbourgs turned those little scenes into full-page pictures of the duke's world: his castles, his court and the peasants who worked his land.

blocks.title: Read a calendar page
blocks.q: The March page of the same book shows a farmer plowing with oxen and others working the fields, below the duke's castle of Lusignan. Why does it look like that?
steps: Each calendar page shows the month's typical work and weather.
In early spring, fields are plowed and sown.
So March shows plowing, with one of the duke's castles behind to say whose land it is.
blocks.a: It shows March's season and labors, on the duke's land.

blocks.html: Thinking medieval art ignored daily life. The calendar pages show feasts, farming and castles season by season. Check the margins and calendars of medieval books: everyday life is everywhere.

blocks.html: In China, landscape painting was the most admired kind of painting for a thousand years. Its Chinese name, shan shui, means "mountain-water." Its great age began under the Song dynasty (960 to 1279), when painters made huge hanging scrolls of towering mountains in ink on silk. They were not painted on the spot: a painter walked and looked for years, then built an ideal landscape from memory and imagination.

Chinese paintings come in formats you hold and unroll. A hanging scroll is tall and hung on a wall for a time. A handscroll is long and low; you unroll it on a table, an arm's length at a time, from right to left. Owners and later collectors added poems and red seals to the painting itself, so a scroll records its own history.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Fan Kuan, Travelers among Mountains and Streams, about 1000, ink and light color on silk, about 2 meters tall. National Palace Museum, Taipei.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Travelers among Mountains and Streams. A huge cliff fills the top two-thirds of the scroll, rising straight up like a wall, its surface built of thousands of small dry brush dots and strokes, like raindrops, that give the rock its texture. A thin waterfall drops down its right side. Mist separates the mountain from the hills below, so we cannot tell how far back it is. At the bottom, tiny travelers drive a train of mules along a path beside a stream. Their smallness makes the mountain immense. In 1958 a scholar found the painter's signature hidden among the leaves at the lower right.
Song dynasty painters such as Fan Kuan (about 1000) and Guo Xi (1072) painted towering mountains in ink on silk, on hanging scrolls and handscrolls.

The painter Guo Xi wrote about the "three distances": the high distance, looking up at a peak from below; the deep distance, looking from the front of a mountain back into the valleys behind it; and the level distance, looking across to far, low hills. A single painting can use all three, so the viewer's eye climbs, wanders and rests instead of staying in one spot.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Guo Xi, Early Spring, 1072, ink and light color on silk. National Palace Museum, Taipei.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Early Spring. Signed and dated by the artist, this scroll shows mountains twisting upward in an S, half lost in spring mist. Trees with crab-claw branches cling to the rocks, and small figures, boats and buildings appear in the valleys if you look closely. The forms blur and sharpen as if fog were moving through them.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Zhang Zeduan, Along the River during the Qingming Festival (detail), early 1100s, handscroll, ink and color on silk. Palace Museum, Beijing.

blocks.html: Zhang Zeduan's handscroll, more than five meters long, follows a river from the countryside into a busy city, with over 800 people: boatmen, shopkeepers, travelers. Scholars debate its exact date and even which city it shows, though most place it in the Northern Song capital, Kaifeng.

blocks.title: Where do you stand?
blocks.q: Looking at Fan Kuan's painting, can you say exactly where the painter stood?
steps: You look up at the great peak (high distance).
You look down on the path and the travelers.
The mist hides the distances between them. There is no single standpoint.
blocks.a: No: the viewpoint shifts on purpose.

blocks.html: Expecting one fixed viewpoint. Chinese landscapes use shifting viewpoints, so you wander through the mountains rather than look from one spot. Check: do the near and far parts follow lines to one vanishing point? Here they do not, by design.

blocks.html: Some of China's greatest art is in bronze, clay and porcelain. Three examples span three thousand years.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Ritual food vessel (ding), Shang dynasty, about 1300 to 1046 BC, bronze. The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

blocks.html: Looking closely: A Shang ding. A round bowl stands on three legs, with two upright handles on the rim. Around the body runs a band of tight, low-relief ornament on a ground of fine spirals; such bands often hold the taotie, a face of two staring eyes, built of animal forms, whose meaning is still debated. Vessels like this held food offered to ancestors in ceremonies, and they were buried with the elite. The green is the color bronze turns after centuries underground. Shang casters did not use lost wax: they built clay molds in sections around a core, carved the ornament into the molds and poured the bronze in.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: A soldier of the Terracotta Army, about 210 BC, painted terracotta. Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor, near Xi'an.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Terracotta Army. In 1974 farmers digging a well near Xi'an struck the first of an army buried to guard the tomb of the First Emperor, who united China in 221 BC and died in 210 BC. Archaeologists estimate about 8,000 life-size soldiers in the pits, with horses and chariots, standing in ranks. This one wears a coat of armor made of small plates; his hair is tied in a topknot. The figures were once brightly painted, and most of the paint flaked off after excavation.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Blue-and-white jar with a dragon, Ming dynasty, early 1400s, porcelain. Jingdezhen kilns. The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

blocks.html: Looking closely: A Ming jar. A sturdy round jar, white as snow, with a scaly blue dragon chasing through clouds around its body and a band of lotus panels at the base. Porcelain is made of a fine white clay called kaolin mixed with china stone and fired at about 1,300 °C, until it is hard, white and glassy. The blue is cobalt, painted under a clear glaze. At Jingdezhen, whole towns of workshops made porcelain for the court and for export across Asia, the Islamic world and, later, Europe, where people simply called it "china."
Shang ritual bronzes (about 1600 to 1046 BC), the Terracotta Army of the First Emperor (about 210 BC) and Ming blue-and-white porcelain span three thousand years of Chinese art.

How can 8,000 figures each look different? The workshops built them like kits: bodies, arms, legs and heads were made in standard parts, some from molds, then assembled. Then the clay was worked by hand: faces, hair, mustaches and armor details were modeled separately, so no two are quite alike. It was mass production with hand finishing.

blocks.name: ar-timeline
blocks.cap: Shang, Qin and Ming on the East Asian timeline.

blocks.title: Put them in order
blocks.q: Order these from oldest to newest: the Ming jar, the Shang ding, a Terracotta Army soldier.
steps: Shang ding: about 1300 to 1046 BC.
Terracotta soldier: about 210 BC.
Ming jar: early 1400s AD.
blocks.a: Shang ding, Terracotta soldier, Ming jar.

blocks.html: Thinking the Terracotta soldiers came from one mold. Their faces, hair and armor vary; workshops combined mold-made parts with hand modeling. Check several figures side by side: no two faces match.

blocks.html: Buddhism began in northern India with the teacher Siddhartha Gautama, called the Buddha, "the awakened one," who lived around the 400s BC. As it spread along trade routes to Central Asia, China, Korea, Japan and Southeast Asia, it carried its art with it, and each region gave that art its own look.

The first great Buddhist monuments are stupas: solid domes of earth and brick holding relics, which pilgrims walk around clockwise. The Great Stupa at Sanchi in central India was begun in the 200s BC, and its four stone gateways, carved around the 1st century BC and AD, are covered with stories of the Buddha's lives.
Buddhist art spread from India across Asia: stupas, robed Buddha figures from Gandhara and Mathura, and temples like Japan's Byōdō-in (1053).

Why do the Sanchi carvings tell the Buddha's story without showing him? In early Buddhist art the Buddha is usually present only through symbols: an empty seat under a tree, a wheel for his teaching, his footprints. Many scholars long explained this as a deliberate avoidance of showing him in human form. Others argue that many of these scenes show people worshiping at holy places, not the Buddha's absence. The debate is not settled.

By the 1st and 2nd centuries AD, artists began to show the Buddha as a person. In Gandhara (in today's Pakistan and Afghanistan), where Greek and Roman art was known, sculptors carved him in gray schist with wavy hair and a monk's robe falling in heavy folds like a Roman toga. At Mathura in northern India, sculptors carved him in red sandstone, with a lighter, thinner robe and a rounder, fuller face. (We describe these in words; we do not have an approved picture yet.)

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Phoenix Hall of the Byōdō-in, Uji, Japan, 1053.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Phoenix Hall. A powerful courtier, Fujiwara no Yorimichi, turned his family's country villa into a temple, and in 1053 built this hall for a gilded statue of Amida, the Buddha of the Western Paradise, carved by the sculptor Jōchō. The hall sits by a pond, with long open corridors spreading to each side like wings, and bronze phoenixes on the roof. Its reflection doubles it in the water. It was meant to look like Amida's palace in paradise, as described in Buddhist scriptures, made real on earth. It appears on Japan's 10-yen coin.

blocks.title: Read the symbol
blocks.q: An early relief shows an empty throne under a tree, with worshipers bowing to it. What might it show, and what is debated?
steps: Many scholars read the empty seat under the tree as the Buddha's awakening, shown by a symbol.
Others read it as people worshiping at the holy site of the awakening.
Either way, the Buddha himself is not shown in human form.
blocks.a: The Buddha's awakening by a symbol, or worship at its site; scholars debate which.

blocks.html: Thinking the Buddha was always shown in human form. Early Buddhist art often showed him through symbols, such as footprints, a tree or a wheel; images of him as a person came centuries after his life. Check the date and place of an image before assuming.

blocks.cap: Gandhara, the Japanese capital region, and Uji.

blocks.html: In the Heian period (794 to 1185), Japan's court lived in the capital Heian-kyō, today's Kyoto. It was a world of poetry, fine silk robes, perfume contests and strict manners, and its women wrote some of its greatest literature. Around 1000, a lady-in-waiting known as Murasaki Shikibu wrote The Tale of Genji, a long story of the loves and sorrows of a prince, often called the world's first novel.

About 1120 to 1140, court painters made a set of illustrated handscrolls of the tale, with passages of beautiful handwriting and paintings in turn. Only fragments survive, now divided between the Tokugawa Art Museum in Nagoya and the Gotoh Museum in Tokyo.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Tale of Genji Scrolls (a scene), about 1130, ink and color on paper. Tokugawa Art Museum, Nagoya.

blocks.html: Looking closely: A scene from Genji. We look down at a steep angle into the palace, as if the roof had been lifted off; Japanese artists call this fukinuki yatai, "blown-away roof." Strong diagonal beams, screens and verandas cut the space into compartments, so figures are seen in separate rooms, near but apart, which suits a story about longing and distance. The courtiers' faces are drawn with a line for each eye and a small hook for the nose (hikime kagibana), so feeling comes through pose, color and setting rather than facial expression. Their robes spread around them in big, flat shapes of color.
Heian court art includes the Phoenix Hall of the Byōdō-in and the 12th-century Tale of Genji handscrolls, seen from above with the roofs "blown off."

Why so little facial expression? At the Heian court, showing strong feeling openly was thought crude. The scrolls show emotion the way courtiers did: through the angle of a body, the colors of layered robes, a poem, an empty room, a season in the garden. The reader is expected to know the story and feel the mood.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Phoenix Hall of the Byōdō-in, 1053, built for a member of the Fujiwara family that dominated the Heian court.

blocks.title: How do you read it?
blocks.q: You are handed a Japanese handscroll in a box. How do you look at it?
steps: Unroll it on a table, not on a wall.
Open about an arm's length at a time, rolling up the part you have seen.
Move from right to left, the direction of Japanese writing then.
blocks.a: Unroll it right to left, a section at a time.

blocks.html: Reading a handscroll like a book page or a wall painting. It is unrolled a section at a time, right to left, so the story unfolds in time as you go. Check the direction: the beginning is at the right end.

blocks.html: Hindu temples are not halls for crowds like churches or mosques. A temple is the home of a god, whose image lives in a small, dark inner room, the sanctum (in Sanskrit garbhagriha, "womb-house"). Above the sanctum rises a tower, and the whole temple is shaped like a sacred mountain, the dwelling of the gods.

In southern India, the Chola king Rajaraja I built the Brihadishvara Temple at Thanjavur, dedicated to the god Shiva and completed in 1010. Its granite tower, the vimana, rises in many stepped stories to about 66 meters, capped by a dome-shaped stone weighing tens of tons, an astonishing feat for its time. Inscriptions on its walls record the gifts the king and his family gave it. (It is described here in words; we do not yet have an approved picture.)
Hindu temples rise like sacred mountains: the Brihadishvara at Thanjavur (completed 1010) and Angkor Wat in Cambodia (1100s).

The mountain idea explains the shape. In Hindu and Buddhist cosmology, Mount Meru stands at the center of the universe, with the gods at its top. A temple tower is a model of that mountain, and the walls and moats around it can stand for the mountain ranges and oceans of the world.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Angkor Wat, Cambodia, first half of the 1100s: the galleries and towers of an inner courtyard.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Angkor Wat. King Suryavarman II of the Khmer Empire built Angkor Wat, beginning in the 1110s, as his state temple, dedicated to the god Vishnu. A huge moat surrounds it, and layer after layer of galleries rises toward five towers shaped like lotus buds, the tallest at the center: Mount Meru with its peaks. In the photograph you see stone galleries with columns, stepped roofs and carved towers around a stone courtyard. The outer gallery holds low reliefs of Hindu epics running about 800 meters around. Unusually, the temple faces west, which may relate to Vishnu or to its role as the king's funerary temple. It is the largest religious monument in the world by area.

blocks.title: Hindu or Buddhist?
blocks.q: Visitors today see Buddhist monks and Buddha images at Angkor Wat. Was it built as a Buddhist temple?
steps: Suryavarman II dedicated it to Vishnu, a Hindu god, in the 1100s.
Later Khmer kings turned to Buddhism, and the temple was gradually adapted.
Buddhist monks have used it ever since, so its use changed over time.
blocks.a: No: it was built as a Hindu temple to Vishnu and later became Buddhist.

blocks.html: Thinking Angkor Wat was always Buddhist. It was built as a Hindu temple to Vishnu and later became a Buddhist site. Check the dates of a building's founding and of its later uses.

blocks.html: Here are four African traditions from four different times and places.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Head from a figure, Nok culture, central Nigeria, more than 2,000 years old, terracotta. Honolulu Museum of Art.

blocks.html: Looking closely: A Nok head. The Nok culture of central Nigeria, among the first in West Africa to smelt iron, made terracotta figures over many centuries of the last millennium BC, into the first centuries AD. This head has heavy, arched brows, triangular eyes with pierced pupils, and a tall, carefully arranged hairstyle. The face is simplified into bold geometric shapes, which make it strong and alert. Dating Nok terracottas is hard because many were dug up by looters without records; that also means some pieces on the market are doubtful.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Head from Ife, Yoruba, 12th to 15th century, copper alloy. British Museum, London.

blocks.html: Looking closely: An Ife head. In the Yoruba city of Ife, artists cast heads in copper and brass by the lost-wax process, as finely as any bronze in the world. This one has a calm, idealized face covered with fine parallel lines, perhaps marks of beauty or rank, and wears a crown with a crest. The surface is smooth and the proportions so natural that some European writers of the early 1900s wrongly credited them to outsiders. They probably portray rulers.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Queen Mother pendant mask (Iyoba), Kingdom of Benin, 16th century, ivory, iron and copper. The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Iyoba mask. In the kingdom of Benin (in today's Nigeria), a guild of carvers worked ivory for the king, the Oba. This small mask, worn at the hip in ceremonies, is thought to portray Idia, mother of Oba Esigie, who ruled in the early 1500s; she was honored for helping him win his throne. Her face is serene, with inlaid iron in the eyes and brow marks, and her crown is a row of tiny carved faces. British forces took it from the royal palace when they captured Benin City in 1897; its twin is in the British Museum.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Great Enclosure, Great Zimbabwe, about 1300 to 1450, granite. A photograph of the early 1900s.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Great Zimbabwe. In southern Africa, ancestors of the Shona people built a capital of stone from about 1100 to 1450. The Great Enclosure is a huge oval wall of granite blocks fitted without mortar, up to about 11 meters high, curving around houses and a solid stone tower. Its rulers grew rich trading gold and ivory to the coast. Colonial writers wrongly credited it to outsiders; archaeology shows it was built by local African people.
Nok terracottas (more than 2,000 years old), the naturalistic Ife heads (12th to 15th centuries), Benin's ivory and brass, and Great Zimbabwe's stone walls show many African traditions.
Why do these works look so different? They come from different peoples, centuries apart, using clay, metal, ivory and stone for shrines, royal ceremonies and a capital city.

blocks.title: Which medium and method?
blocks.q: Which of these was cast by lost wax: the Nok head, the Ife head, or the Iyoba mask?
steps: The Nok head is fired clay (terracotta): modeled, not cast.
The Iyoba mask is ivory: carved.
The Ife head is copper alloy: cast by lost wax.
blocks.a: The Ife head.

blocks.html: Thinking of "African art" as one timeless style. Africa's arts come from many cultures, dates, named workshops and histories. Check the date, the place and the people for each work, as you would for a European one.

blocks.html: Mesoamerica, from central Mexico through Central America, built cities, writing, calendars and pyramids with no contact with the Old World. Its peoples shared maize farming, a sacred ball game, a 260-day ritual calendar and stepped pyramids topped by temples.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Colossal Head from San Lorenzo, Olmec, about 1200 to 900 BC, basalt. National Museum of Anthropology, Mexico City.

blocks.html: Looking closely: An Olmec head. The Olmec of the Gulf Coast of Mexico carved huge heads from single boulders of basalt; seventeen are known, ranging from about 1.5 to over 3 meters tall and weighing many tons. This one has a broad face, full lips, a wide nose and heavy-lidded eyes under a close-fitting helmet with a band across the forehead. Each head has a different face and headgear, which is why scholars think they portray particular rulers. The stone came from mountains many kilometers away, so moving it took great organization.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Pyramid of the Sun, Teotihuacan, about AD 200. A photograph of about 1900.

blocks.html: Teotihuacan, near today's Mexico City, was one of the largest cities in the world around AD 500, with perhaps 100,000 people or more. Its Pyramid of the Sun, finished around AD 200, is about 65 meters tall, built of rubble and adobe faced with stone.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: El Castillo, Chichén Itzá, Maya, about 900 to 1100. A photograph of about 1900.

blocks.html: Looking closely: El Castillo. The Maya built cities of limestone across southern Mexico and Central America and wrote in a full system of glyphs. At Chichén Itzá, this pyramid of nine stepped terraces has a stairway on each side, each with 91 steps; with the top platform, that makes 365, the days of the solar year. At the spring and autumn equinoxes, the afternoon sun casts a zigzag of shadow on the north stair that looks like a serpent sliding down to the carved serpent heads at its base. At Palenque, the Temple of the Inscriptions held the tomb of King Pakal, who died in 683; it was found in 1952.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The Aztec Sun Stone, about 1502 to 1520, basalt, about 3.6 meters across. National Museum of Anthropology, Mexico City.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Sun Stone. The Aztecs (Mexica) ruled from Tenochtitlan, today's Mexico City. This huge disk, about 24 tons, has a face at the center, usually identified as the sun god, surrounded by rings: the four earlier ages of the world, the twenty day-signs of the calendar, and two great fire-serpents around the rim. It was found in 1790 in Mexico City's main square.
The Olmec carved colossal basalt heads (about 1200 to 900 BC); the Maya built Palenque and Chichén Itzá and wrote in glyphs; the Aztecs carved the great Sun Stone (about 1502 to 1520).

Why call it the "Calendar Stone"? It carries the day-signs of the calendar, so early writers assumed it was one. But it could not be used to count days, and scholars debate what it was: an altar for ceremonies, a monument to the sun and the ages of the world, or both.

blocks.title: Calendar or not?
blocks.q: Is the Aztec Sun Stone a working calendar?
steps: It carries the twenty day-signs and symbols of the ages of the world.
But it has no means of counting or tracking particular days.
Scholars debate its use: an altar, a monument to the sun, or both.
blocks.a: No; it carries calendar signs, but its use is debated.

blocks.html: Calling the Aztec Sun Stone a working calendar. It carries calendar signs, but scholars debate its use; it may have been a ceremonial altar or a monument. When scholars disagree, say so instead of picking one answer.

blocks.html: In South America, cultures of the Andes mountains and the Pacific coast built cities, roads and irrigation, and made superb pottery, textiles and goldwork. In North America, peoples of the Southwest and the Mississippi valley built villages and towns of stone and earth.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Machu Picchu, Peru, Inca, about 1450. An early photograph.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Machu Picchu. The Inca ruled the largest empire in the Americas from Cusco. Machu Picchu was probably a royal estate for the emperor Pachacuti, built around 1450 on a ridge high above the Urubamba River, with the peak of Huayna Picchu rising behind. Terraces step down the slopes for farming and to hold the soil. Inca masons fitted the stones of the finest walls without mortar, so tightly that a knife blade will not slip between them, and they tilted walls and doorways slightly inward, which helps them stand through earthquakes. The site was little known outside the region until the explorer Hiram Bingham publicized it in 1911.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Portrait vessel of a ruler, Moche, Peru, about 100 BC to AD 500, painted ceramic. The Art Institute of Chicago.

blocks.html: Looking closely: A Moche portrait vessel. The Moche of Peru's north coast made jars in the shape of human heads, so lifelike that they seem to be portraits of particular men. This one has a strong jaw, a steady gaze and lines around the mouth, and wears a patterned headdress and big ear ornaments. The arched handle on top is a stirrup spout, a Moche specialty. Some were made in molds, so the same face could appear on several vessels.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Cliff Palace, Mesa Verde, Colorado, Ancestral Puebloan, about 1190 to 1260. A photograph of the early 1900s.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Cliff Palace. Under a great overhang of sandstone, the Ancestral Puebloans built a village of shaped stone blocks set in mortar: about 150 rooms, square and round towers, and 23 kivas, round sunken rooms for ceremonies and gatherings. Tree-ring dates from its wooden beams show it was built mostly between about 1190 and 1260 and lived in until about 1280. Today it is part of Mesa Verde National Park.

Farther east, people of the Mississippian culture built Cahokia, near today's St. Louis, the largest town north of Mexico, at its height about 1050 to 1350. Its Monks Mound, an earthen platform about 30 meters high, is the largest prehistoric earthwork in the Americas.
The Inca fitted stones without mortar at Machu Picchu (about 1450); the Moche made portrait vessels; Ancestral Puebloans built Cliff Palace at Mesa Verde (about 1190 to 1260).

How do we date Cliff Palace so precisely? Its builders used wooden beams, and tree rings grow one per year, wide in wet years and narrow in dry ones. Matching a beam's ring pattern to a long master sequence tells the year the tree was cut. This is the same method, dendrochronology, used to date the oak panels of Flemish paintings.

blocks.title: Why no mortar?
blocks.q: Inca walls in an earthquake zone have no mortar. How can that help?
steps: The stones are shaped to fit tightly, and the walls lean slightly inward.
In a quake the stones can shift a little and settle back without the wall collapsing.
Mortared walls can crack and fall apart instead.
blocks.a: Tightly fitted, slightly tilted stones can move and resettle.

blocks.html: Thinking ancient America had no great builders. Inca masonry, Puebloan cliff dwellings and Mississippian mounds say otherwise. Check what survives: roads, terraces, towns and monuments across two continents.

blocks.html: Italian painting around 1280 still followed the Byzantine "Greek manner": flat, gold-ground, long-faced figures, like the icons you met in Icons. Then a Florentine painter, Giotto di Bondone (about 1267 to 1337), began painting figures that look solid and heavy, standing on the ground in real space and showing real feeling. Writers from Dante to Vasari praised him as the painter who brought painting back to nature.

His masterpiece is the Arena Chapel (also called the Scrovegni Chapel) in Padua, painted about 1303 to 1305 for the banker Enrico Scrovegni. Its walls hold a cycle of true frescoes in rows, telling the stories of Mary's parents, of Mary and of Christ, under a vault painted deep blue with gold stars.

blocks.name: ar-artwork

hotspots.label: Joachim
hotspots.text: Sent away from the temple, he walks with head bowed, wrapped in his cloak.

hotspots.label: The shepherds
hotspots.text: They glance at each other, unsure how to greet him.

hotspots.label: The dog
hotspots.text: The only one glad to see him.

hotspots.label: The rocky stage
hotspots.text: A simple ledge of rock, like a stage set, holds the figures.

hotspots.label: The blue sky
hotspots.text: Not gold, but a blue sky.

blocks.cap: Giotto, Joachim among the Shepherds, about 1305, fresco. Arena (Scrovegni) Chapel, Padua.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Joachim among the Shepherds. Joachim, Mary's father, has been turned away from the temple, and he comes to his shepherds in shame. He is a block of pink cloak, heavy and still, his head bowed; we feel his weight on the ground. The two shepherds look at each other, not at him: an awkward moment we all know. Only the little dog jumps up in welcome. The setting is simple: a rocky ledge, a few trees, a hut, a flock, and a blue sky instead of gold. There is no clutter; every shape helps tell the feeling.
In the Arena Chapel in Padua (about 1305), Giotto painted solid, weighty figures with real feeling, a break from flat Byzantine style.

How does Giotto make figures look solid? He models each robe with light and shadow, as if lit from one side, so it reads as a rounded mass. He sets figures on a ground line in a shallow space with a few objects to fix where they stand. And he often places figures with their backs to us, which a flat icon never does: we sense that the space continues behind them.

blocks.name: ar-compare
blocks.cap: Duccio's Maestà (A, Siena, 1308 to 1311) and Giotto's fresco (B, Padua, about 1305).

blocks.title: Byzantine or Giotto?
blocks.q: A painting has a gold background, a large frontal Virgin, and rows of saints stacked up the sides. Another has a blue sky, a rocky ledge and figures turning toward each other. Which is closer to Giotto?
steps: Gold ground and frontal, stacked figures belong to the Byzantine tradition.
A real sky, a ground to stand on, and figures relating to each other are Giotto's innovations.
blocks.a: The second.

blocks.html: Thinking the Renaissance began suddenly in 1400. Giotto's solid figures a century earlier pointed the way, and some art historians call his era the Proto-Renaissance. Check the dates of the "firsts" you read about.

sources.name: National Core Arts Standards, Visual Arts, High School (Responding: perceive, analyze and interpret artistic work)

blocks.html: How do you paint a flat picture that looks like a window onto a deep room? Roman painters had suggested depth by eye, and Giotto by solid figures. In Florence around 1415 to 1420, the architect Filippo Brunelleschi showed a mathematical answer. He painted a small panel of the Baptistery as seen from the cathedral door, drilled a hole in it, and had viewers look through the back at a mirror held in front: the reflected painting lined up with the real building. In 1435 the scholar Leon Battista Alberti wrote down the method in his book On Painting.

items: Horizon line: a horizontal line at the viewer's eye level.
Vanishing point: a point on the horizon where lines running straight away from the viewer seem to meet.
Orthogonals: those receding lines (floor tiles, the tops of walls, a table edge), all aimed at the vanishing point.
Objects shrink at a steady rate as they go back, so you can measure how big a far figure should be.

blocks.name: ar-persp
blocks.cap: One-point perspective. Drag the horizon and the vanishing point.

blocks.html: Brunelleschi showed how lines going back meet at one vanishing point (about 1415 to 1420), Alberti wrote the method down (1435), and Masaccio used it in paint.

Why do parallel lines seem to meet? Things look smaller the farther away they are. Two rails a meter apart take up less and less of your view as they recede, until far off the gap is too small to see. Perspective drawing measures that shrinking exactly. Alberti compared the picture to a window: paint what you would see through the glass from one fixed eye.

blocks.name: ar-artwork

hotspots.label: Christ's head
hotspots.text: The building's receding lines meet here: the vanishing point.

hotspots.label: The building
hotspots.text: Its edges are orthogonals, slanting toward Christ.

hotspots.label: Peter, again
hotspots.text: At the left, Peter takes a coin from a fish's mouth.

hotspots.label: And again
hotspots.text: At the right, Peter pays the tax collector.

hotspots.label: Hazy mountains
hotspots.text: Far hills are paler and bluer: atmospheric perspective.

blocks.cap: Masaccio, The Tribute Money, about 1425 to 1427, fresco. Brancacci Chapel, Florence.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Tribute Money. A tax collector, his back to us, demands payment. In the center Christ, among his apostles, points to the lake; at the left Peter kneels there and finds a coin in a fish's mouth; at the right he pays the collector. One picture holds three moments: a continuous narrative. The apostles stand like heavy columns in a circle around Christ, lit from the right, each casting a shadow, and the building's lines run back to Christ's head. Masaccio died at about 27, but this fresco shaped Florentine painting for a century.

blocks.title: Find the vanishing point
blocks.q: In Leonardo's Last Supper, the lines of the ceiling, the walls and the tapestries all slant toward the center. Where do they meet?
steps: Follow the ceiling beams and wall edges inward.
They meet at Christ's head, at the center of the painting.
The point that organizes the space is also the focus of the story.
blocks.a: At Christ's head.

blocks.html: Thinking no one showed depth before the Renaissance. Roman painters suggested depth with overlapping and haze, as in Livia's garden room. What was new was a mathematical system with a single vanishing point. Check: depth cues are old; one-point construction is the Renaissance invention.

sources.name: Leon Battista Alberti, On Painting (De pictura), 1435

blocks.html: Florence's cathedral, Santa Maria del Fiore, was begun in 1296 with a plan for a huge dome over an eight-sided crossing about 45 meters wide. By 1418 the walls were up to the base of the dome, but no one knew how to build it. A dome that wide would normally be built over centering: a wooden framework holding up the masonry until it was complete. There was not enough timber in Tuscany to build one that size, and the city did not want Gothic flying buttresses.

In 1418 the city held a competition. Filippo Brunelleschi, a goldsmith turned engineer, won with a plan to build the dome without full centering. Work ran from 1420 to 1436; the marble lantern on top was finished later, after his death in 1446.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The dome of Florence Cathedral, by Filippo Brunelleschi, 1420 to 1436.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The dome. From the hills above Florence, the dome rises over the roofs like a red mountain, larger than anything around it. Eight white marble ribs climb from the drum to the lantern, dividing the red tile into eight curved panels. It is pointed rather than round in profile, a shape that pushes out less at the base. The lantern on top, a small temple of white marble, locks the ribs together and lets light into the space below.
Filippo Brunelleschi raised the dome of Florence Cathedral from 1420 to 1436 without full wooden centering, using a double shell and herringbone brick.

How did it stand while it was being built? The dome is two shells, an inner and a lighter outer one, tied together by ribs. The bricks were laid in a herringbone pattern: every so often a brick stands on end, locking each new ring of horizontal bricks so it cannot slide inward before the mortar sets. Each completed ring is a closed circle that holds itself up. Chains of stone and timber, and iron, run around the base like hoops on a barrel to resist the outward push. Brunelleschi also invented an ox-powered hoist to lift the materials.

blocks.name: ar-map
blocks.cap: Florence, with Rome to the south.

blocks.title: Why not buttresses?
blocks.q: A Gothic cathedral holds up its vault with flying buttresses outside. How does Florence's dome resist its outward push instead?
steps: Its pointed profile pushes outward less than a round dome would.
Hoop-like chains around its base hold it in, the way hoops hold a barrel.
Its double shell and ribs make it strong but lighter.
blocks.a: With its shape, internal chains and a double shell, not flying buttresses.

blocks.html: Thinking the dome is held up by buttresses. It has no flying buttresses; its double shell, ribs, chains and brick patterns carry it. Check the outside of the building: you see the dome rising straight from its drum.
Brunelleschi had studied ancient buildings in Rome, including the Pantheon. His dome is wider and higher than the Pantheon's, and it is still the largest masonry dome in the world.

blocks.html: Florence in the 1400s was a city of bankers, wool merchants and guilds, and they competed to pay for art. Sculptors, painters and architects studied ancient Roman ruins and the new rules of perspective, and the result is called the Early Renaissance ("rebirth," meaning the rebirth of ancient learning).

In sculpture, Lorenzo Ghiberti spent 27 years, from 1425 to 1452, making a pair of gilded bronze doors for the Baptistery of Florence, with ten large square panels of Bible stories. Michelangelo, it is said, called them worthy to be the Gates of Paradise, and the name stuck. Ghiberti used perspective in metal: figures in front stand out in high relief, while buildings and hills behind sink into low relief, so a few centimeters of bronze look deep. The originals are now in a museum; copies hang on the Baptistery. (We do not have an approved picture of them yet.)

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Donatello, Equestrian Statue of Gattamelata, 1445 to 1453, bronze. Padua.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Gattamelata. Donatello made this monument to a soldier, Erasmo da Narni, nicknamed Gattamelata, for the city of Padua. Rider and horse are cast in bronze and stand high on a pedestal. The horse steps forward, one front hoof resting on a ball; the rider sits straight and calm in armor, holding a commander's baton. It was the first large bronze horse and rider cast in Italy since ancient times; Donatello knew the Roman bronze of the emperor Marcus Aurelius in Rome.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Fra Angelico, The Annunciation, about 1440 to 1445, fresco. Convent of San Marco, Florence.

blocks.html: The friar-painter Fra Angelico placed his Annunciation in a porch whose slender columns and arches follow the new perspective and the new architecture of Brunelleschi.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Piero della Francesca, Portraits of the Duke and Duchess of Urbino, about 1473 to 1475. Uffizi Galleries, Florence.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Piero's portraits. Piero della Francesca, who also wrote on mathematics and perspective, painted the duke and duchess of Urbino in strict profile, like heads on ancient Roman coins, against a landscape that stretches for miles in soft light. Every form is simplified and clear: the duke's red hat is almost a geometric solid.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Sandro Botticelli, Portrait of a Man with a Medal of Cosimo the Elder, about 1474 to 1475. Uffizi Galleries, Florence.

blocks.html: Ghiberti's Gates of Paradise, Donatello's bronze Gattamelata, Fra Angelico's Annunciation and Piero della Francesca's portraits brought the new realism to Florence and beyond.

Why so many portraits now? Wealthy citizens and rulers wanted to be remembered as individuals, as the ancient Romans had been. Medals, busts and painted portraits spread. In Botticelli's portrait, a young man holds up a medal of Cosimo de' Medici, the banker who ruled Florence in all but name: a sign of loyalty to the family. Who the young man was is unknown.

blocks.title: Painting or relief?
blocks.q: A friend says Ghiberti's Gates of Paradise are the finest paintings in Florence. Correct the claim.
steps: They are doors, made of bronze, cast and then gilded.
Their scenes are reliefs, raised from the surface, not painted.
They use perspective by changing how high the relief stands.
blocks.a: They are gilded bronze reliefs, not paintings.

blocks.html: Mixing up Ghiberti's doors with a painting. They are gilded bronze reliefs that use perspective in metal. Check the medium on the label before you describe a work.

blocks.html: Leonardo da Vinci (1452 to 1519) trained in Florence, worked for the duke of Milan, and ended his life in France. He was a painter, engineer, inventor and student of nature, and his notebooks, about 7,000 pages survive, are full of studies of water, plants, machines, light and flight. Yet only some fifteen to twenty paintings are generally accepted as his, and several of those were left unfinished.

blocks.name: ar-artwork

hotspots.label: The vanishing point
hotspots.text: The lines of the ceiling and walls meet at Christ's head.

hotspots.label: The window
hotspots.text: The bright window behind Christ frames his head like a halo.

hotspots.label: Groups of three
hotspots.text: The apostles react in four groups of three.

hotspots.label: A later door
hotspots.text: A doorway was cut through the bottom of the wall in the 1600s.

blocks.cap: Leonardo da Vinci, The Last Supper, about 1495 to 1498, tempera and oil on dry plaster. Santa Maria delle Grazie, Milan.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Last Supper. Leonardo painted it for the dining hall of a monastery in Milan, for the duke Ludovico Sforza, so the monks ate below Christ and his apostles at their own long table. The moment is Christ's words, "One of you will betray me." The apostles recoil, question and argue in four groups of three, a wave of motion, while Christ sits still at the center, his body a calm triangle. Leonardo used the room's architecture: all the lines of the painted room lead to Christ's head, and the window behind him makes a natural halo. He painted slowly on a dry wall, and the paint began to flake within decades.

blocks.name: ar-artwork

hotspots.label: The smile
hotspots.text: The corners of the mouth melt into shadow, so the expression seems to change.

hotspots.label: The left horizon
hotspots.text: The landscape on the left sits lower...

hotspots.label: The right horizon
hotspots.text: ...than on the right. The two sides do not quite match.

hotspots.label: The hands
hotspots.text: Relaxed and softly modeled, one resting on the other.

blocks.cap: Leonardo da Vinci, Mona Lisa, begun about 1503, oil on poplar. Louvre, Paris.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Mona Lisa. A woman sits half-length, turned three-quarters toward us, her hands folded on the arm of a chair, in front of a wild landscape of rocks, water and a winding road. There are no hard outlines anywhere: edges dissolve in soft shadow. Leonardo called this blending "without lines or borders, in the manner of smoke"; we call it sfumato, from the Italian fumo, "smoke." She is usually identified as Lisa Gherardini, wife of a Florentine merchant. Leonardo kept working on it for years and never delivered it; the Louvre dates it 1503 to 1519.
Leonardo painted the Last Supper (about 1495 to 1498) and the Mona Lisa (begun about 1503), using sfumato: soft, smoky transitions without hard outlines.

Why does sfumato make a face seem alive? Our eyes read expression mostly from the corners of the mouth and eyes. Leonardo buried exactly those corners in soft shadow, so the brain has to fill them in, and it fills them in a little differently each time we look.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Leonardo da Vinci, Lady with an Ermine, about 1489 to 1490, oil on walnut. Czartoryski Museum, Kraków.

blocks.title: Why did it decay?
blocks.q: The Mona Lisa, painted in oil on wood, is in good condition. The Last Supper, from the same years, was flaking within decades. Why?
steps: Leonardo did not paint the Last Supper in true fresco.
He used tempera and oil on a dry wall, so the paint did not bond with the plaster.
Damp in the wall lifted the paint.
blocks.a: It was painted on dry plaster, not in true fresco.

blocks.html: Thinking Leonardo finished many paintings. Only about fifteen to twenty survive that are generally accepted as his, and several were left unfinished. Check the "attributed to" labels: experts still debate a few.

blocks.html: In the early 1500s, Rome replaced Florence as the center of Italian art, because the popes paid for it. Two artists dominated: Raphael (1483 to 1520), from Urbino, and Michelangelo Buonarroti (1475 to 1564), from Florence. The period of about 1490 to 1527, with Leonardo, Raphael and Michelangelo, is called the High Renaissance.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Raphael, Portrait of Baldassare Castiglione, about 1514 to 1515, oil on canvas. Louvre, Paris.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Raphael's Castiglione. Raphael's friend Baldassare Castiglione, a diplomat who wrote The Book of the Courtier, a famous guide to graceful behavior, sits turned three-quarters toward us, his hands folded. The colors are almost all grays, blacks and soft whites: a fur-trimmed gray doublet, a black hat, a white shirt, a warm gray background. The pyramid of his body is calm and stable, and his blue eyes meet ours directly. Everything is relaxed and effortless, exactly the grace Castiglione wrote about. Rubens and Rembrandt later studied this portrait.

Raphael ran a large workshop in Rome and painted frescoes for the popes in the Vatican palace, along with altarpieces and portraits. His figures are graceful and his compositions balanced, so for centuries teachers held him up as the model of perfect harmony. He died at 37.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: The dome of St. Peter's Basilica, Vatican City, designed by Michelangelo from 1547; completed by Giacomo della Porta in 1590.

blocks.html: Looking closely: St. Peter's dome. When Michelangelo took charge of rebuilding St. Peter's in 1546 to 1547, he was over seventy. He designed a dome on a tall drum ringed with paired columns, with sixteen ribs rising to a lantern. He studied Brunelleschi's dome in Florence for it. He did not live to see it built; Giacomo della Porta completed it in 1590, with a somewhat taller, more pointed profile. It still dominates the skyline of Rome.
Raphael painted calm, graceful portraits and frescoes in Rome; Michelangelo was a sculptor, painter and architect who designed the dome of St. Peter's.

Why call Michelangelo a sculptor first? He trained in marble and signed letters "Michelangelo, sculptor." He thought of carving as freeing a figure already inside the stone. Even his paintings look carved, their figures as solid as statues. Late in life he worked mostly as an architect, in Florence on the Laurentian Library and in Rome on St. Peter's and the Capitoline Hill.

blocks.name: ar-compare
blocks.cap: Raphael (A) learned from Leonardo (B): the three-quarter pose and folded hands.

blocks.title: Who did what?
blocks.q: Match the artist: (1) the portrait of Castiglione; (2) the design of the dome of St. Peter's; (3) the Mona Lisa.
steps: (1) Castiglione's friend Raphael painted his portrait.
(2) Michelangelo designed the dome; della Porta finished it.
(3) Leonardo painted the Mona Lisa.
blocks.a: (1) Raphael, (2) Michelangelo, (3) Leonardo.

blocks.html: Thinking Michelangelo was mainly a painter. He called himself a sculptor, and late in life he worked mostly as an architect. Check the works by medium: marble statues, a few great fresco cycles, and buildings.

blocks.html: Venice, a rich trading republic built on islands in a lagoon, had its own tradition of painting. Venetian painters took up oil paint early: Giovanni Bellini was using it by the later 1400s, and the Sicilian painter Antonello da Messina, who knew Netherlandish oil technique, worked in Venice in 1475 to 1476. By 1500 Venetians often painted on canvas, which suited the damp air better than fresco did, and they built pictures from color and light.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Giovanni Bellini, Doge Leonardo Loredan, about 1501 to 1502, oil on poplar. National Gallery, London.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Doge Leonardo Loredan. The doge, elected ruler of Venice, appears behind a stone ledge like a portrait bust, against a deep blue background. His ceremonial robe is cloth of gold and silver damask, with big buttons like bells, and every thread seems to catch the light. His face is lit from the left: thin, wise, a little amused, the wrinkles and veins painted with soft glazes. A small paper label on the ledge gives Bellini's name in Latin. Bellini built the image layer by layer, so the colors glow from within.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Titian, Portrait of a Man, about 1510, oil on canvas. National Gallery, London.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Titian's man in blue. A young man turns to look at us over his shoulder, his elbow on a ledge, his huge quilted sleeve of shimmering blue filling the front of the picture. The silk is painted with loose, quick touches of light and dark rather than sharp lines: up close it is almost brushwork alone; from a few steps back it becomes satin. Titian (about 1488 to 1576) was Bellini's pupil and became the most sought-after painter in Europe. The sitter is uncertain; he was once called the poet Ariosto, and some think he is Titian himself.
Venetian painters such as Giovanni Bellini and Titian built pictures from rich color and oil glazes rather than line, often painting on canvas in the damp lagoon air.

In the 1500s, art writers framed a contest between disegno and colorito. The Florentine biographer Giorgio Vasari praised disegno: drawing and design, the idea worked out in line before painting. Venetians were famous for colorito: building form directly with color, light and the brush. The debate was partly city pride, but it names a real difference you can see.

blocks.name: ar-compare
blocks.cap: Rome (A, Raphael) and Venice (B, Titian): both relaxed portraits; compare the handling of the sleeves.

blocks.title: Florence or Venice?
blocks.q: A portrait has crisp contours, a carefully drawn design and smooth surfaces. Another has soft edges, glowing color and visible, loose brushwork in the cloth. Which is more Venetian?
steps: Crisp contours and drawing first: disegno, the Florentine and Roman ideal.
Soft edges and form built from color and brush: colorito, the Venetian way.
blocks.a: The second.

blocks.html: Thinking Florence and Venice painted the same way. Florence prized drawing (disegno); Venice prized color (colorito). Check the edges and the brushwork: line or color?

blocks.html: While Florence studied ancient Rome, painters in the wealthy trading cities of Flanders, such as Bruges and Ghent, led another revolution: oil painting on oak panels, used with a precision no one had seen. The leader was Jan van Eyck (about 1390 to 1441), court painter to the Duke of Burgundy.

Oil paint dries slowly and can be laid on in very thin, transparent layers called glazes. Light passes through the glazes and reflects off the white ground beneath, so colors glow like stained glass. Painting with tiny brushes, these artists could show the texture of fur, the shine of brass, the reflection in a mirror and the fall of light through a window.

blocks.name: ar-artwork

hotspots.label: The mirror
hotspots.text: A convex mirror reflects the whole room, and two figures at the door.

hotspots.label: The chandelier
hotspots.text: Every curl of brass catches the light.

hotspots.label: The window
hotspots.text: Light from the left falls on oranges on the sill.

blocks.cap: Jan van Eyck, The Arnolfini Portrait, 1434, oil on oak. National Gallery, London.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Arnolfini Portrait. A merchant, usually identified as Giovanni di Nicolao Arnolfini, and a woman stand in a room in Bruges. Van Eyck shows things no Italian of 1434 was painting: the curve of a mirror that bends the whole room into a circle, light glinting on each brass arm of the chandelier, the separate hairs of a little dog. Above the mirror he wrote, "Jan van Eyck was here, 1434," as if he were a witness. What exactly the scene records (a marriage, a betrothal or a memorial) is debated.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Rogier van der Weyden, Portrait of a Lady, about 1460, oil on panel. National Gallery of Art, Washington.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Rogier's Lady. A young woman, her eyes lowered, wears a sheer white headdress pinned into a wide frame. The thin cloth is painted so we see her forehead through it. Against the dark background her pale face, the red belt and her clasped hands form a simple design. Rogier van der Weyden of Brussels was the other great Netherlandish master; who the sitter was is unknown.

blocks.name: ar-artwork

hotspots.label: The stretched shape
hotspots.text: Seen from the right side, close to the wall, it becomes a skull: a reminder of death.

hotspots.label: Instruments
hotspots.text: Globes, sundials and a quadrant: the learning of the age.

hotspots.label: The lute
hotspots.text: One of its strings is broken.

blocks.cap: Hans Holbein the Younger, The Ambassadors, 1533, oil on oak. National Gallery, London.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Ambassadors. Two Frenchmen in London, the diplomat Jean de Dinteville and the bishop Georges de Selve, stand beside a shelf of instruments: a celestial globe, sundials, a terrestrial globe, a lute, a hymnbook. Across the floor slants a strange gray shape. Viewed from close to the right edge, it snaps into a skull, a technique called anamorphosis. Holbein seems to say: all this learning and wealth, and death is waiting.
Jan van Eyck's Arnolfini Portrait (1434) shows what oil glazes could do: tiny details, glowing color and a convex mirror reflecting the room.

Why is a north-European oil painting so detailed? Slow-drying oil let painters work for weeks on tiny areas, and transparent glazes let them build up depth of color. Oak panels, prepared with a smooth chalk ground, gave a hard, flat surface for the finest brushes.

blocks.title: Who invented oil paint?
blocks.q: A guidebook says Jan van Eyck invented oil painting. Correct it.
steps: Oil-based paints were known for centuries before him.
Van Eyck and other Netherlandish painters perfected the use of thin, layered glazes.
So he was a master of oil technique, not its inventor.
blocks.a: He perfected oil glazing; he did not invent oil paint.

blocks.html: Thinking Van Eyck invented oil paint. Oil was known before him; he and other Netherlandish painters perfected layered glazes. Check "first" and "invented" claims; they are often legends.
