blocks.html: Printing changed art as much as it changed books. After Gutenberg's press in the 1450s, an artist could make a design once and sell hundreds of copies across Europe. Albrecht Dürer (1471 to 1528) of Nuremberg, in Germany, was the first artist to become famous everywhere through prints. He signed them with his monogram, a large A with a small D under it.

head: Woodcut
Engraving
rows: The artist cuts away everything that should print white, leaving the lines raised
The artist cuts the lines into the metal with a sharp tool (a burin)
In the cut grooves (an intaglio print); the surface is wiped clean
Very fine lines and delicate shading
blocks.cap: The two print techniques Dürer mastered.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Albrecht Dürer, The Rhinoceros, 1515, woodcut. Impressions in many museums, such as the National Gallery of Art, Washington.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Rhinoceros. In 1515 an Indian rhinoceros arrived in Lisbon, the first seen alive in Europe in centuries, a gift to the king of Portugal. Dürer never saw it. Working from a written description and a sketch sent to Nuremberg, he drew a beast covered in plates like armor, with scales on its legs and a small extra horn on its back. The bold black lines of the woodcut make it monumental. It is wrong in many details, yet it was so convincing that it was copied in books for centuries.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Albrecht Dürer, Young Hare, 1502, watercolor and gouache on paper. Albertina, Vienna.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Young Hare. Dürer also studied nature directly. This hare crouches on bare paper, every hair painted with a fine brush: light and dark fur, long whiskers, ears turned back. A tiny glint in its eye may be the reflection of a window, as if it were sitting in his studio.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Albrecht Dürer, Self-Portrait at Twenty-Eight, 1500, oil on panel. Alte Pinakothek, Munich.

blocks.html: Albrecht Dürer of Nuremberg made woodcuts and engravings that sold across Europe, like his Rhinoceros (1515), and watercolors such as the Young Hare (1502).

Why prints? A painting lives in one place and costs a great deal. A print can travel by the hundred in a merchant's bag. Prints made Dürer wealthy and famous, and they spread images and styles faster than ever before: Italian artists copied Dürer's designs, and Dürer learned from Italian art on his trips to Venice.

blocks.title: Which kind of print?
blocks.q: A print has strong, bold black lines, and the paper shows a slight raised texture where the inked surface pressed. The block was wood. What kind of print is it?
steps: Wood, cut so the lines stand up: a relief block.
Ink on the raised lines: a woodcut.
blocks.a: A woodcut.

blocks.html: Mixing up woodcut and engraving. A woodcut prints the raised parts of a carved block; an engraving prints ink held in lines cut into metal. Check the material and where the ink sits: on top (woodcut) or in the grooves (engraving).

blocks.html: Pieter Bruegel the Elder (about 1525 to 1569) worked in Antwerp and Brussels, in the Netherlands then ruled by Spain. He began designing prints for a publisher, traveled to Italy, and became the great painter of the Flemish countryside and its people: peasants at work and at feasts, proverbs acted out, and the seasons of the year.
In 1565 he painted a series of the months or seasons for the house of an Antwerp merchant and collector, Niclaes Jongelinck. There were probably six panels; five survive.

blocks.name: ar-artwork

hotspots.label: The hunters
hotspots.text: Tired men and dogs plod home with only a fox to show.

hotspots.label: The fire
hotspots.text: At the inn, people singe a pig over a fire.

hotspots.label: The skaters
hotspots.text: Tiny figures skate and play on the frozen ponds.

hotspots.label: Mountains
hotspots.text: Jagged peaks no Flemish landscape has: Bruegel had crossed the Alps.

hotspots.label: A bird
hotspots.text: A single bird glides across the cold sky.

blocks.cap: Pieter Bruegel the Elder, Hunters in the Snow, 1565, oil on oak. Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Hunters in the Snow. The hunters and their dogs trudge downhill at the left, their dark shapes sharp against the snow. A line of trees leads the eye down and to the right, out over the valley: frozen ponds full of skaters, villages, a mill with a frozen wheel, and far mountains. The colors are almost all white, black and a cold green-gray. You feel the cold and the long day. The picture is both a landscape of huge depth and a story of ordinary lives.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Pieter Bruegel the Elder, The Harvesters, 1565, oil on wood. The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Harvesters. Summer in the same series: workers cut wheat with scythes, tie sheaves, carry jugs, and rest under a pear tree for lunch, one man stretched out asleep. Behind them the land opens to a hazy bay. The gold of the wheat fills half the picture. Bruegel shows the work and the rest of farm life with affection and without making it pretty.
Pieter Bruegel the Elder painted peasants, seasons and landscapes, such as Hunters in the Snow and The Harvesters (both 1565).

These pictures descend from the calendar pages of books like the Très Riches Heures, where each month had its labors. Bruegel made them full-size panel paintings for a collector's walls, and he made the landscape itself the subject.

blocks.title: Who was Bruegel?
blocks.q: A visitor says Bruegel was a peasant painting his own village. Check the evidence.
steps: He worked in the cities of Antwerp and Brussels and traveled to Italy.
He designed prints for a city publisher and knew learned men.
His patrons were wealthy collectors like Niclaes Jongelinck.
blocks.a: He was an educated city artist painting peasant life for rich collectors.

blocks.html: Thinking Bruegel was a peasant painting his own village. He was an educated city artist whose patrons were wealthy collectors. The nickname "Peasant Bruegel" came from his subjects and from a story told by an early biographer. Check who made a work and for whom, not only what it shows.

blocks.html: Renaissance architects wanted to build like the ancient Romans. They measured ruins such as the Pantheon, read the Roman architect Vitruvius, and revived the classical orders, round arches, domes and, above all, clear proportions: simple ratios like 1 to 1 and 1 to 2 that make every part fit the whole.

items: Filippo Brunelleschi built the first great Renaissance buildings in Florence in the 1420s, with round arches on slender Corinthian columns and spaces measured in simple ratios.
Leon Battista Alberti designed church fronts based on Roman temples and triumphal arches.

Andrea Palladio (1508 to 1580) built palaces, churches and country villas around Vicenza and Venice and published them in The Four Books of Architecture (1570), which spread his designs across Europe and to America.

blocks.name: ar-arch
blocks.cap: Romanesque (A), Gothic (B) and Renaissance (C) church fronts.

blocks.html: Renaissance architects revived Roman columns, round arches and domes with clear proportions; Palladio's Villa La Rotonda (begun about 1567) was copied for centuries.

Why proportion? Renaissance thinkers believed, following Vitruvius, that good buildings, like the human body and musical harmonies, are made of parts in simple ratios. A room twice as long as it is wide, or a façade whose height equals its width, feels calm and complete. Symmetry around a central axis adds to the sense of order.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Andrea Palladio, Villa La Rotonda, near Vicenza, begun about 1567: his own plan and section, from The Four Books of Architecture, 1570.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Villa La Rotonda. Palladio designed this villa on a hilltop for a retired churchman, Paolo Almerico. The plan you see is a square with a round hall at its center under a dome, and an identical temple-front porch, with columns and a pediment, on each of the four sides, so the house looks the same from every direction and opens to views all around. Every room is measured to fit the whole like a puzzle. Palladio died before it was finished; Vincenzo Scamozzi completed it.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Thomas Jefferson, Monticello, Charlottesville, Virginia, 1769 to 1809. A photograph from the Historic American Buildings Survey.

blocks.html: Palladio's book crossed the Atlantic. Thomas Jefferson owned it and drew on Palladian ideas, among others, for his house, Monticello, with its columned porch and central dome. You will meet it again in Neoclassicism.

blocks.title: Renaissance or Gothic?
blocks.q: A church front is symmetrical, with flat columns supporting a triangular pediment and a round-arched doorway. Which style?
steps: Pointed arches and spires would mean Gothic.
Columns, a pediment and round arches are classical.
Symmetry and clear proportion fit the Renaissance.
blocks.a: Renaissance.

blocks.html: Mixing Renaissance and Gothic façades. Renaissance buildings use symmetry, round arches, columns and pediments; Gothic ones use pointed arches, tracery and spires. Check the shape of the arches first.

blocks.html: After about 1520, many artists in Italy turned away from the calm balance of the High Renaissance. They stretched proportions, crowded or flattened space, twisted poses, and used cool, shimmering or unusual colors. Art historians later named the style Mannerism, from the Italian maniera, "style" or "manner": for the art writer Giorgio Vasari, writing in 1550, maniera was a term of praise for refined, graceful artifice.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Agnolo Bronzino, Eleonora of Toledo with Her Son Giovanni, about 1545, oil on panel. Uffizi Galleries, Florence.

blocks.html: Looking closely: Eleonora of Toledo. Bronzino, court painter to the Medici dukes of Florence, painted Duchess Eleonora, wife of Cosimo I, with one of her sons. She sits stiff and upright against a flat blue background, her face smooth and pale as porcelain, her expression cool and distant. Her gown, gold and black brocade with a pattern of pomegranates, is painted thread by thread and seems more alive than she is. The portrait is about rank and dynasty, not personality: a perfect, polished, unapproachable image.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: Sofonisba Anguissola, The Chess Game, 1555, oil on canvas. National Museum, Poznań, Poland.

blocks.html: Looking closely: The Chess Game. Sofonisba Anguissola of Cremona painted three of her younger sisters at a game of chess, watched by their governess. The sister at the left looks out at us, about to win; the youngest grins; the sister at the right lifts her hand in surprise. It is a portrait of a family moment, warm and lively, in rich costume. Anguissola became so admired that she later served at the court of Philip II of Spain.

blocks.name: ar-artwork
blocks.cap: El Greco, View of Toledo, about 1599 to 1600, oil on canvas. The Metropolitan Museum of Art.

blocks.html: Looking closely: View of Toledo. El Greco ("the Greek," Domenikos Theotokopoulos, 1541 to 1614) was born on Crete, trained as an icon painter, studied in Venice and Rome, and settled in Toledo in Spain. Here the city climbs its hill under a stormy sky of torn clouds and flashes of light. The greens are unnatural and vivid, and he moved the cathedral tower to a place it does not really stand. It is less a map than a vision of the city. El Greco is often grouped with Mannerism, but his style is so personal that many scholars treat him as a case of his own.
After about 1520, Mannerist artists stretched proportions, crowded space and used cool, strange colors; Bronzino's portraits and El Greco's View of Toledo show the range.

Why turn away from balance? Many reasons are offered: artists who had studied Raphael and Michelangelo wanted to go beyond them; courts prized elegance and display; and times were troubled, with Rome sacked by imperial troops in 1527 and Christendom divided by the Reformation. Scholars weigh these differently.

blocks.title: High Renaissance or Mannerist?
blocks.q: One portrait is relaxed and warm, the sitter turned toward us in a stable pyramid. Another shows a sitter stiff and remote, with porcelain skin, against a flat blue ground, her gown more vivid than her face. Which is Mannerist?
steps: The first describes Raphael's Castiglione: High Renaissance balance and warmth.
The second describes Bronzino's Eleonora: cool, polished, artificial.
blocks.a: The second.

blocks.html: Thinking Mannerist distortion was a lack of skill. These artists could draw "correctly" and chose elegance and strangeness on purpose. Check: does the same artist draw hands, cloth and faces with complete control? Then the distortion is a choice.
